title: Without Jensen Huang, Nvidia's organizational structure isn't 'built to last,' management expert says
summary: Nvidia's flat management structure could pose challenges for Huang's successor, according to experts.
body: Jensen Huang resigned Thursday as CEO of Nvidia , the chipmaking company he co-founded in 1993, following public revelations of his extramarital affairs. Colette Kress, Nvidia's chief financial officer, will serve as the company's interim CEO . Huang's visionary leadership style and his central role in driving the company's strategy, combined with the company's unusually flat management structure, will make him especially difficult to replace, experts say. Huang notably had more direct reports than the typical CEO, with a "direct staff" of approximately 60 employees, he said in a March 2026 interview with podcaster Lex Fridman. "The more direct reports a CEO has, the less layers are in the company. It allows us to keep information fluid," Huang told CNBC's Andrew Ross Sorkin in 2023. Having minimal hierarchy has worked for Nvidia so far "because [Huang] has been a strong leader with a strong vision," says Jo-Ellen Pozner, associate professor of management at Santa Clara University's Leavey School of Business. But that structure could make the company's leadership shake-up even more difficult to navigate, she says. At companies with flat management structures, the CEO often has even more influence than they would in a traditional hierarchy, according to Joseph Fuller, professor of management practice at Harvard Business School. Nvidia's structure was "designed to adapt well in a world of change, either caused by us or affecting us," Huang said in a March 2025 conversation with Arthur Mensch, cofounder and CEO of Mistral. Since he directly managed the company's top executives, Huang held "a tremendous amount of power" at Nvidia, Fuller says. "He's the orchestrator," he continues. "He's the coordinator. He's resolving the disputes. He's allocating the resources." Now, the company has lost its top decision-maker, Fuller says. Without Huang, "there is likely nobody who is able to coordinate among those various people with their different expertise and domains," Pozner says, which could lead to a slowdown in technical work. There are some advantages to Nvidia's flat structure, says Denise Rousseau, professor of organizational behavior and public policy at Carnegie Mellon University. Having fewer management layers can strengthen "local leaders" in each area of the company, she says, which can help stabilize Nvidia through its leadership transition. But "nobody else has the big picture view" that Huang did, Pozner says, which makes finding a permanent successor within the company especially difficult. Moreover, with dozens of direct reports, it's unlikely that Huang had the time to groom one of his subordinates to take over one day, she says. Pozner predicts that Nvidia's next leader will steer the company toward a more traditional management structure. "I understand that a lot of people, especially in Silicon Valley, are averse to rigid hierarchies and the kind of structure that we expect from a legacy organization," she says. "But it's functional for a reason." Ultimately, Nvidia's current system is "not an organizational structure that's built to last," Pozner says. title: Cisco beats on earnings, says AI infrastructure revenue will double this fiscal year
summary: Cisco is trying to become a bigger player in AI after missing out on the early years of the boom.
body: Cisco shares rose in extended trading on Thursday after the maker of networking gear reported better-than-expected fiscal first-quarter results. Here's how the company did compared to LSEG consensus estimates: Revenue increased 24% from $14.88 billion a year earlier, Cisco said in a statement. Net income rose to $4.6 billion, or $1.14 per share, from $2.9 billion, or 72 center per share, a year ago. Cisco is trying to gain a foothold in the artificial intelligence buildout after missing out on the early years of the generative AI boom. The company's stock price is up about 35% this year as of Thursday's close, trouncing the Nasdaq, which has gained 9% over that stretch. Cisco raised its expectation for AI infrastructure revenue from hyperscalers to $9 billion this fiscal year, more than double the figure in fiscal 2026. "Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era," CEO Chuck Robbins said in the statement . For the fiscal second quarter, Cisco said it expects revenue of between $18 billion and $18.2 billion, topping the average analyst estimate of $17.88 billion, according to LSEG. The company is projecting adjusted earnings per share of $1.34 to $1.36, beating the $1.23 average estimate.

title: United Airlines won’t let AI agents book your flight. Expert says you shouldn't let a bot do that for you, anyway
summary: AI agents can save you time, but an expert says decisions involving your health, wealth and privacy still need human input.
body: United Airlines said Wednesday it would be restricting artificial intelligence bots from its digital platforms, warning that allowing third-party AI assistants to access account credentials could expose sensitive personal information, lead to unintended purchases or other unauthorized account activity. The move is similar to Amazon's recent blocking of Meta's Muse agent from making purchases on its site. Still, AI agents can complete a wide range of tasks on your behalf. Instead of just asking Muse what the weather will be tomorrow, you can tell it to suggest an outfit based on tomorrow's weather forecast and book you a rideshare if it's going to rain, for example. Or, rather than just creating an itinerary for your next vacation, you can connect a payment option and have your Dot — OpenAI's agent offering — book flights, hotels and excursions for you. You can even have an AI agent buy and sell stocks through investing platforms like Robinhood. Relying on an AI agent for any of these tasks may come with mixed results depending on which agent you use, what data you allow it to access and the complexity of the task you've asked it to carry out. Because broadly, agentic AI is still in its infancy, you may not want to let an agent make decisions "anytime [your] health, wealth, or privacy are involved," says Shomit Ghose, adjunct professor at the University of San Francisco School of Management, and lecturer at the University of California, Berkeley College of Engineering. "You can have agents do interesting things for you, like categorize your spending, or flag unusual charges, or model what-if scenarios," he says. "Those are good things, but bad things would be moving money, making trades, filing forms. All those things should stay manual at this point." Here's what you should consider before outsourcing your whole to-do list to an AI agent. Though AI agents' capabilities are improving, they still operate in a fairly literal sense, which can create problems, Ghose says. If you tell your agent to book you the cheapest flight, for example, it may book you a flight at 3 a.m. or one with three layovers, unless you give the agent specific guardrails. "The bot only knows your context," Ghose says. "It cannot infer, as we humans are able to do, because of instinct and culture and education." Further, bots can still get it wrong even with a seemingly clear and direct command. They "treat all data as being equal," Ghose adds. So if it finds information on the web that is either inaccurate or subjective, it could give you misleading guidance or fail to meet your standards for the given task. For example, if you tell your agent to book you a reservation at a good barbecue restaurant, it may get you a table at a place that claims to be "the best barbecue in the world" on its website. But the restaurant may be in an inconvenient location or have poor reviews elsewhere on the web. Your command may need to be more specific, like asking your agent to check reviews on Google Reviews or Yelp. Depending on what task you've assigned the bot, the outcome could be rather innocuous. But when individuals consider letting bots make purchases for them, make changes to their investment portfolios or and the like, the result could be more consequential. "In the end, you want to ask yourself: Does the human need to be in the loop?" Ghose says. If you're booking a vacation, for example, it's reasonable to ask an AI agent to help make a decision on your destination based on the weather, your budget and other factors. But actually booking the flights and hotels "should still come back to me," Ghose says. He wants to maintain final say over major financial decisions. Doing so may even save you money. In Booking Holdings ' third-quarter earnings report, the Connecticut-based travel technology company reported 20% higher spending among customers who used AI assistants versus those who didn't to book accommodations on Agoda, one of its travel platforms. title: Alice Huang tied to Nvidia’s biggest Chinese competitor
summary: The woman with whom Jensen Huang reportedly had a relationship also owned stakes in companies that provided computing power to Huawei, a key Nvidia competitor.
body: Alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang may have owned stakes in businesses in China that benefited Nvidia's biggest competitor in China, Huawei, at the same time that she was in business with Nvidia and also reportedly having a romantic affair with its ousted CEO Jensen Huang . The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei was first discovered by analysts at private intelligence firm Tesari. The firm exclusively shared its findings with CNBC. Tesari, which uses artificial intelligence to collect evidence and specializes in national security investigations around the world, provides intelligence research to private companies and the U.S. government. This previously unreported entanglement may raise questions about Alice Huang's intent and conduct in her relationship with the CEO and whether Jensen Huang knew his romantic partner was closely connected with his competition. Jensen Huang has acknowledged having an affair, though the precise timing of his relationship with Alice Huang is unknown. The mysterious saga of Alice Huang involves a tangle of interlocking corporations and transactions that show her connection to entities that ultimately provided computing power to Huawei in China. Huawei is known as a Chinese government "state champion" in the technology and telecommunications sectors, meaning it receives enormous financial support from the government in Beijing so it can lower prices and undercut global competitors. It is considered a key part of the Chinese government's push for global technical dominance and is closely linked to the Chinese Communist Party. Businesses connected to Alice Huang were linked with supplying Nvidia computing power to Huawei, according to documents reviewed by CNBC, around the same time she and Jensen Huang were first publicly seen together, in December 2023. In 2024, Nvidia said Huawei was a top competitor , specifically in artificial intelligence chips including graphics processing units, central processing units and networking chips. "This activity, which surfaced through our analysis of Alice's network, warrants a national security and [technology] counterproliferation investigation," said Brian Andersen, Tesari's vice president for national security applications and a former supervisory special agent with Homeland Security Investigations. If the Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry Security and Homeland Security Investigations found evidence that anyone transferred "controlled equipment" to Huawei without authorization, potential charges might include export-control violations, conspiracy and smuggling, Andersen said. The connection between Alice Huang and Huawei is so convoluted that analysts at Tesari told CNBC that based on their previous investigative experience, they suspect it was designed to deliberately obscure the relationship. Nvidia and Huawei did not respond to CNBC's requests for comment. Jensen Huang did not respond to a voicemail left on a mobile phone. Alice Huang could not be reached. According to Chinese corporate records and media reports compiled by Tesari and provided to CNBC, Alice Huang, whose Chinese name is Huang Le and who according to documents at the time was based in Hong Kong, in 2019 sold a cloud business she owned called Osmanthus to a Chinese gaming company called 7Road. A subsidiary of 7Road, which was based in Singapore, was spun off as "Megaspeed" in 2023 . Megaspeed would go on to become a key Nvidia customer, helping facilitate at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese firms, The Information reported Tuesday. As early as 2016, Alice Huang had also become a co-owner of a financial firm known as Shanghai Hexi , which heavily invests in tech and data centers. In 2021, Hexi in turn acquired 27 percent of a company called Shanghai Century Longteng, a data center developer, which Hexi held until 2024 . title: Jensen Huang is out and Nvidia stock is down—what market pros say about buying dips
summary: Nvidia stock fell 5% on Thursday following the departure of CEO Jensen Huang. Some see it as a signal to sell, others an opportunity to buy.
body: Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang has resigned as the firm's president and CEO, the company announced Thursday. Investors reacted negatively to the news. By 2:30 p.m., shares of the chipmaking giant were down more than 5%, and now sit 31% below their high on October 6. It's easy to see why Huang's departure, which comes amid revelations of his romantic ties to a woman believed by the U.S. intelligence community to be a Chinese spy , has investors feeling queasy. The company Huang co-founded 33 years ago — and whose chips have powered the artificial intelligence boom — has grown into the firm currently valued at about $4 trillion under his leadership. "The premise here is that there is no successor to a generational founder," says Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of the Founders 100 ETF, which invests in founder-led companies. "It's that they're one of one, and what they bring from a vision, execution and grit standpoint is not replaceable." While some investors are exiting Nvidia positions based on that premise — Monaghan's fund must, per its prospectus — others will see the slip in Nvidia's price as an opportunity to buy a great stock on proverbial sale , he says. Looking purely at the numbers, the opportunity to buy a stock with Nvidia's prodigious projected growth at its current depressed price "happens once a decade, maybe once in a career as an investor," he says. In investing parlance, the latter group of investors is " buying the dip " — investing in an asset after a decline in its value in anticipation of a bounceback. Whether it's a prudent strategy for you with Nvidia or any other stock requires some examination, investing experts say — not only of the stock in question, but your own portfolio strategy. When an investment you own or are interested in declines, your first move is to examine your reason for buying or holding it, says Tom Hainlin, national investment strategist at U.S. Bank Asset Management. Ask yourself if whatever caused the slide has changed your investment narrative, he says. "Has it changed why I bought the stock or why I'm investing in the market?" If you own a diversified portfolio and the broad U.S. stock market has declined, buying dips is a relatively straightforward decision, investing pros say. Because the stock market has historically trended upward, each downdraft has offered investors an opportunity to add an appreciating asset at a discount. "If you have a solid, long-term investment, it's always attractive to buy the dip because you always get a new high," Jeff Buchbinder, chief equity strategist with LPL Financial, told Make It in August. "In the history of the S&P 500, every dip has been attractive because you eventually made new highs." Individual stocks have no such track record, meaning that a major slide should prompt you to re-examine the thesis behind any given investment, Hainlin says. That analysis is twofold. On one hand, you should rethink the position any one stock occupies in your portfolio. If it's a large enough chunk that a pullback is keeping you up at night, it might be worth paring the position back to put things more in line with your tolerance for risk, he says. And whether you own the stock or are thinking about buying, a dip is a good time to evaluate your outlook for that investment. If you plan to hold a particular stock for the long term, for instance, you'll have to weigh whether the short-term bad news could have a lasting impact on the firm's profitability. "Did Nvidia's prospects change as a result of [Huang's resignation]? There's no definitive answer for that," he says. Monaghan says that, based on historical data, there may be reason to worry. His fund's fact sheet cites data from consultancy Bain & Company showing that founder-led companies vastly outperformed their peers from 1990 through 2014. title: In a policy switch, the Fed says its October 2027 meeting will not see a vote on interest rates
summary: Fed Chair Kevin Warsh announced the move at his October news conference, though he did not set a date.
body: The Federal Reserve won't vote on a potential interest-rate change at its October 2027 meeting, a departure that is part of a broader initiative from Chairman Kevin Warsh aimed at reducing the central bank's market footprint. According to an announcement Thursday, the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee will set aside its Oct. 26-27 session for "the discussion of broad monetary policy strategy issues." Warsh announced the move at his news conference after the FOMC met in October, though he did not specify which meeting would be affected. In 2027, there will be seven voting meetings, with the October session set up as extra time for policy deliberation without a formal vote or post-meeting statement. The new calendar shows that the final meeting of the year will now take place in November. It had previously been set for December. "Now, what's the reasoning behind this change? To me, it's quite straightforward," the chairman said in explaining his rationale. "Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals." "But it's equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations—for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point," he said. Warsh has been critical of the Fed's prior communications strategy, saying policymakers spent too much time providing guidance on policy moves that handcuffed them when it came time to make decisions. Under typical practice, the Fed meets eight times a year, following with a vote on interest rates and then a news conference from the chair. Since Warsh took over, the post-meeting statement has been shortened dramatically. Moreover, the press question-and-answer sessions have been cut to around half an hour from their customary 45 minutes or so. Warsh said in October that the meeting schedule is another step in his plan to streamline communication. He indicated last month that the number of nonvoting meetings would increase to two in 2028. "I believe the setting of the meeting schedule and agenda is more than some administrative detail," he said. "It's an institutional choice, affecting the nature and the quality of our deliberations and, ultimately, the wisdom of our decisions. It's yet another change to get the conduct of monetary policy on the right track." The FOMC next meets Dec. 8-9. Its first meeting in 2027 will happen Jan. 26-27. Correction: The Fed's October 2027 meeting will not see a vote on interest rates. The headline in an earlier version misstated the year.

title: Here's what Colette Kress and Harvey Jones wrote to Nvidia employees
summary: Interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones emailed Nvidia employees, expressing gratitude for "resilience, professionalism and continued dedication
body: On the heels of founder Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO of Nvidia , new interim CEO Colette Kress and board chair Harvey Jones sent emails to employees Thursday expressing gratitude and optimism for the future. CNBC obtained copies of the emails from a source familiar with the matter, who said Jones sent the first email and Kress replied shortly after. Follow CNBC's live coverage of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation "The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication," Kress wrote in her email. The term Estaff is commonly used to refer to executive staff, the group of direct reports to C-suite executives at a company. Nvidia will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PST, her email said. Board chair Jones took a similar tone in his email, and praised Kress as "a key architect of NVIDIA's growth and capital strategy." "The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you," Jones wrote. I believe deeply in this company and in its future. More than anything, I believe in each of you, in our customers and partners and in the vital role we play every day in the global economy. The Board, Estaff and I recognize that this has been an extraordinarily difficult period and I want you to know how grateful we are for your resilience, professionalism and continued dedication. Thank you. This company has achieved so much because of the work that all of you bring to it every single day. You are our greatest strength. You will hear more from leadership in the coming days about our future together, and we will host a company meeting on November 18 at 9am PT. We play a vital role in building the technology that is powering the AI revolution, and we have important work ahead of us. So let's move forward together, with the same determination and commitment that have always defined this company. I am writing to share an important update. Jensen has resigned as CEO and Board Member, and the Board has asked our Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress to serve as interim CEO while it conducts a search for a permanent successor looking at both internal and external candidates. I will serve as the first-ever Chair of the Board. As CFO for over 13 years, Colette has been a key architect of NVIDIA's growth and capital strategy. She possesses a deep understanding of this business and the markets in which we operate. The Board has full confidence in Colette to deliver on our commitments to shareholders, customers, partners, and to each of you. Jensen's contributions to NVIDIA are profound. NVIDIA is one of the most consequential technology companies in the world. We pioneered accelerated computing, defined the modern GPU, and built the platform that powered artificial intelligence. The Board takes seriously our duty as stewards of this great company. The strength of this company resides in our employees, leadership team, technical strength and partner ecosystem. I am confident that under Colette's leadership, with the full support of the Board, we will continue to grow our business, and lead the industry forward. Thank you for your focus, your professionalism, and your commitment to NVIDIA.

body: A PMI still well above 50 gives little reason to doubt New Zealand’s recovery, so the small fall should do little to change the outlook for the RBNZ or the New Zealand dollar. The focus on fuel prices among survey respondents links New Zealand’s factory sector to the oil shock. That keeps input costs and inflation pressure in view, even as demand holds up. Election uncertainty is a near-term drag on business confidence that could weigh on investment decisions until a coalition is formed. Markets will look to Monday’s services index for a fuller read on domestic momentum. New Zealand’s factory expansion lost a little pace in October but held a solid footing, as Christmas demand and infrastructure work offset rising fuel costs and post-election uncertainty. New Zealand’s manufacturing sector kept expanding in October, though more slowly than in September’s strong result. The seasonally adjusted BNZ-BusinessNZ Performance of Manufacturing Index (PMI) fell 1.4 points to 54.9 from 56.3, BusinessNZ said on Friday. A reading above 50 means the sector is expanding and below 50 that it is contracting. October was a 16th straight month above that line. The detail was mixed but still solid. Deliveries rose to 61.4, and finished stocks were 58.0, just below September. New orders slipped to 54.3 from 56.8 and production fell to 53.9 from 56.6, but both remain well inside expansion territory. Employment was again the weakest component at 51.9, almost unchanged from September. BusinessNZ’s director of advocacy, Catherine Beard, welcomed more than a year of unbroken expansion. She said the softening in new orders and production was worth watching. She also said the Christmas build-up and steady infrastructure work suggest manufacturers will finish the year on a solid footing, even as input costs and the cost of living weigh on many firms. Survey comments turned a little gloomier. The share of negative comments rose to 56.4% from 53% in September. Respondents cited fuel prices, the cost of living and uncertainty following the general election. BNZ said election uncertainty is likely to linger until final results are in and coalition talks are settled. The regional picture was uneven. Business South had the strongest reading at 65.0, ahead of Canterbury at 57.9 and the EMA’s northern region at 55.5. The Business Central region slipped into contraction at 49.1. BNZ said every manufacturing subindustry expanded in October. The bigger picture is still positive. BNZ said the result supports its forecast of moderate manufacturing growth through the fourth quarter and annual GDP growth of around 2% in 2026. Its senior economist said that although the PMI moves around from month to month, momentum in manufacturing is firmly positive. New Zealand’s reading also compares well internationally. It matches the US and is above the global manufacturing PMI of 52.6. The services index, due on Monday, will show whether the slower pace is limited to manufacturing. title: Japan’s Katayama warns of one-sided yen moves near 160, will coordinate with US Treasury
summary: Katayama’s comments make intervention a more serious risk for anyone pushing dollar-yen above 160, especially as the US has now been confirmed as a willing partner. Expect choppy, headline-driven trading around that level, with dealers alert to any reports of rate checks. The underlying pressure on the yen remains, though, as rising Fed hike expectations keep rate differentials in the dollar’s favour. Oil matters too: higher crude prices raise Japan’s import bill and add to selling pressure on the yen, which is partly why Tokyo is bringing forward energy subsidies. --- Earlier: US Treasury bought yen in July, its first intervention since 1998, as yen nears 160 again --- With the yen back near 160, Katayama is reminding markets that Tokyo and Washington are working together on currencies, and that both have intervened before. body: Katayama’s comments make intervention a more serious risk for anyone pushing dollar-yen above 160, especially as the US has now been confirmed as a willing partner. Expect choppy, headline-driven trading around that level, with dealers alert to any reports of rate checks. The underlying pressure on the yen remains, though, as rising Fed hike expectations keep rate differentials in the dollar’s favour. Oil matters too: higher crude prices raise Japan’s import bill and add to selling pressure on the yen, which is partly why Tokyo is bringing forward energy subsidies. With the yen back near 160, Katayama is reminding markets that Tokyo and Washington are working together on currencies, and that both have intervened before. Main article: Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama stepped up her warnings over the yen’s slide, saying she is seeing one-sided and rapid moves in currency markets and will stay in contact with the US Treasury to respond appropriately. Her comments come as the yen trades back near 160 per dollar, the level that drew joint US-Japan intervention in the summer. Katayama said the US and Japan set out a shared stance on foreign exchange at their summit, signalling that Tokyo sees Washington as aligned on the need to curb disorderly moves. She declined to comment on intervention records. That came shortly after the New York Fed disclosed that the US Treasury bought yen in July, its first yen-buying intervention since 1998, acting alongside Japan’s Ministry of Finance. The wording matters. Japanese officials typically use terms like “one-sided” and “rapid” when their concern is growing. Naming coordination with the US Treasury adds weight, because Washington has now shown it is willing to put its own money behind the yen. Japan’s vice finance minister for international affairs, Atsushi Mimura, gave a similar message on Thursday, warning that it was too early to forget the summer’s intervention. The yen’s renewed weakness reflects a familiar gap. A resilient US economy, stubborn inflation and rising expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike in December are supporting the dollar. The Bank of Japan, which raised rates in June and September, is widely expected to hike again in December. Until that gap narrows, officials are relying on words, and the threat of action, to slow the yen’s fall. Katayama also said the government has decided to bring forward subsidies for household utility bills this winter, paid for from reserve funds. The move aims to protect households from high energy costs. Elevated oil prices have pushed those costs up, and the weak yen makes them worse, because Japan imports almost all of its energy. For markets, the comments make it riskier for traders to push dollar-yen through 160. With both Tokyo and Washington signalling they are ready to act, the risk of another round of intervention is likely to keep the pair volatile around that level in the weeks before the BOJ’s December meeting. body: $7 Billion in Oil Debt Has Nigerian Banks Holding Back Lending What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… Oil prices have crashed about 20% from the late-October peak of $118 per barrel, weighed down by hopes of sustainable de-escalation in the Middle East and the Russia-Ukraine war. For months, traders and hedge funds have often bet on a resolution of the conflicts, only to reactivate buying when talks fall apart. As U.S.-mediated talks between Ukraine and Russia are underway, there are no signs of a breakthrough in either the conflict in Europe or the U.S.-Iran standoff, despite messaging via Qatar. Oil prices have slipped as crude oil flows from the Strait of Hormuz and the entire Middle Eastern region have rebounded in recent weeks to nearly pre-war levels. But Brent at about $94 a barrel on Thursday, after briefly slipping below $90 on Wednesday, could be very close to a floor under oil prices if the Middle East remains the gray area of ‘no deal but no escalation either’ for months. As long as the stalemate persists, risks to shipping will remain elevated and insurance premiums will stay high, adding sharply to the cost of each barrel of crude oil that is able to leave the Strait of Hormuz. Middle Eastern benchmarks have been weakening for weeks, suggesting an oil glut may be building amid rebounding Persian Gulf exports and global demand destruction amid high prices. Related: Ukraine Peace Talks Yield Prisoner Deal but No Path to Peace But the costs to refiners and consumers are not falling. War, insurance premiums, and record tanker rates pushed the cost of shipping a barrel of crude from the Middle East Gulf to Asia on a large tanker to more than $37 by mid-October, more than five times the pre-war level, according to the International Energy Agency . The current pause in high-intensity strikes in the Middle East doesn’t mean the risk of escalation and energy shocks are over. Significantly increased crude oil flows don’t mean traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has suddenly become less dangerous. In fact, attacks on vessels have intensified in the past month, with 37 attacks on ships in and near the Strait of Hormuz in October alone, the highest monthly tally since the war began on February 28, according to Washington Institute for Near East Policy data cited by Reuters . At least 10 more ships were hit in the first 10 days of November. At the same time, Gulf producers are tying up a large portion of the global tanker fleet on inefficient shuttle movements in and out of the Strait and subsequent ship-to-ship (STS) transfers in the Gulf of Oman. Then there is also a risk of re-escalation despite signals from U.S. President Donald Trump from early this week that no further strikes on Iran are necessary at present. The President, however, noted that the U.S. remains “locked and loaded” in case a new military campaign becomes necessary. Trump sounded less patient on Thursday. In a Truth Social post, he said the United States does not need a deal with Iran because Washington already has Iran’s money and, in his words, “we’ve got their Strait.” Brent climbed more than 1% to around $94 a barrel after the post, according to CNBC . The ball is in the American court now, as Iran waits for Washington’s response to its seven conditions to start peace talks, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, Iran’s top negotiator and Parliament Speaker, told Al Jazeera in an exclusive interview on Wednesday. The conditions on which Iran has insisted for months include lifting of the U.S. blockade in the Gulf of Oman, ending of fighting on all fronts, and the release of the frozen Iranian funds. summary: Venezuela is opening up its electricity sector to private capital for the first time since Hugo Chávez nationalized it in 2007, in a reform passed this week primarily to benefit oil producers and large businesses that can afford euro-pegged tariffs, while the state keeps the hydroelectric dams and main transmission lines that supply most households living with daily blackouts. body: $7 Billion in Oil Debt Has Nigerian Banks Holding Back Lending Alex Kimani is a veteran finance writer, investor, engineer and researcher for Safehaven.com. Venezuela is opening up its electricity sector to private capital for the first time since Hugo Chávez nationalized it in 2007, in a reform passed this week primarily to benefit oil producers and large businesses that can afford euro-pegged tariffs, while the state keeps the hydroelectric dams and main transmission lines that supply most households living with daily blackouts. The law, which the National Assembly passed unanimously on Tuesday, lets oil producers build power plants for their own fields without state authorization, as long as those plants stay off the national grid. Other private generators need a concession from the Ministry of Electric Energy for any plant above 50 megawatts. National Assembly president Jorge Rodríguez, the interim president’s brother, said those generators will sell mainly to large consumers, at tariffs the government has yet to publish. Households that cannot pay the full price keep a subsidized rate on a state grid that experts estimate generates about 12,000 megawatts, against demand that reached 16,400 MW in September. Their best prospect for more power is the repair deal with GE Vernova and Argentina’s Impsa, and Caracas has yet to guarantee payment to the suppliers it needs for that work. Aging terminals, crude-quality problems and grid failures held Venezuela’s oil exports near 1.25 million bpd through the summer, with tankers waiting as long as 30 days to load. Repsol, which holds 40% of the Petroquiriquire joint venture with PDVSA on Lake Maracaibo, had launched open requests to source its own power plants and supplies by May, Reuters reported . Power expert Miguel Lara told Reuters at the time that he did not know “which power supply will support the economic reactivation they are talking about.” Venezuela’s US-backed oil expansion will need power that does not depend on the grid. On August 31, the White House announced that North American Blue Energy Partners, a privately held company controlled by Venezuelan businessman Alejandro Betancourt, had received 100-year concessions over 17 fields in the Lake Maracaibo region and the Orinoco Belt. The fields hold about 65 billion barrels of proven reserves, roughly a fifth of Venezuela’s total. The company has given the Pentagon’s Office of Strategic Capital a 35% stake in its parent and says it will invest up to $100 billion in new oil infrastructure. Chevron pumps about 290,000 bpd in Venezuela and plans to spend more than $7 billion through 2031 to raise that to about 600,000 bpd. The country as a whole produces 1.1 million to 1.2 million bpd. Outside the oilfields, the law lets private and mixed-ownership companies generate, transmit, distribute and sell power through joint ventures of up to 25 years. A new superintendency will oversee tariffs, service and self-generation, and the law offers guarantees to private participants whose terms have not been published. Siemens Energy and GE Vernova met Venezuelan officials in April to discuss grid repairs. The government, citing legal obstacles, rejected a proposal from foreign firms seeking prepayment for initial repairs and spare parts. Promissory notes Caracas had issued to suppliers in the past went unpaid, and many were sold at steep discounts. “They still have no clue on how we would get paid,” an executive at one equipment supplier told Reuters. Interim President Delcy Rodríguez said on October 8 that the government plans to add 7,400 MW through its agreements with General Electric and Impsa, and 600 MW from unit 6 of the Planta Centro power station in partnership with China. Lara puts the cost of stabilizing the grid at no less than $15 billion over three years. body: $7 Billion in Oil Debt Has Nigerian Banks Holding Back Lending Haley Zaremba is an energy journalist and researcher with more than a decade of professional experience covering global energy systems, land and natural resources, and… Another month, another distressing Consumer Price Index report. As the war in Iran drags on, inflation in the United States is remaining stubbornly high, driven in large part by sky-high food and energy costs. Overall, prices rose four-tenths of a percent over the last month, and are expected to finish the year at a four percent increase as compared to 2025 – a blistering increase that reflected itself at the polls in last week’s midterm elections, where a blue wave has largely been viewed as a rebuke of Trump, his war in Iran, and his policies’ overall impact on the economy. At the same time, despite relatively strong jobs numbers, wages have remained stagnant. “That paints a dreary picture for Americans struggling with high costs, who likely won't feel any relief at the pump in the near future — especially as more potential military action looms [in Iran],” Business Insider reported in response to October’s Consumer Price Index report. “For everyday Americans, all of these international strains amount to what is, essentially, a pay cut,” the article goes on to say. In an interview with PBS News, Austan Goolsbee of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago spoke with a high degree of concern about the persistence of inflation in the economy, indicating that ongoing impacts from the war in Iran are to be expected – especially where high energy prices are concerned – but says that other impacts, such as high prices from tariffs, should have faded by now. And, worryingly, they simply have not. “Now, what we have been dealing with is a series of shocks – some from oil prices, some from tariffs, now some from the demand side, and a lot of those things were supposed to go away,” Goolsbee told PBS. “And they might still go away and prove transitory, but whenever you start hearing the word transitory, the hair on your neck should be standing up a little bit, because we went through that, where it was supposed to go away. And we found out that, when you have major disruptions to the supply chain, those oftentimes end up being far more persistent than [...] the theory says they're supposed to be.” The demand-side issues that Goolsbee refers to include the mounting issue of skyrocketing energy demand to power the artificial intelligence boom, which has pushed energy prices even higher in the regions of the country experiencing data center hyperscaling. The sector has an overall inflationary effect beyond energy rates as well, as the bailout boom drives up costs for a wide range of services and goods including construction, computers, electrical equipment, and computer chips. While these inflationary impacts have been widely seen as a result of the Trump administration’s leadership, as exemplified by last week’s stunning midterm election blowout in favor of Democratic candidates, the issues extend far beyond the reach of a single political regime. Instead, according to Tim McDonnell, the climate and energy editor for the nonpartisan news outlet Semafor, the issue is that oil and gas, the stalwart energy resources that made the United States the premier global superpower, are no longer a reliable source of energy security. “The inherent volatility of oil and gas prices is a persistent vulnerability in the US economy that can only be solved by limiting exposure to these energy sources,” McDonnell wrote in an op-ed leading up to the mid-term elections. “Domestic drilling has put more of the supply-demand balance under US control, but can’t shield American consumers from global price turmoil,” he goes on to say. body: $7 Billion in Oil Debt Has Nigerian Banks Holding Back Lending Julianne Geiger is a veteran energy journalist and market analyst with more than a decade of experience covering the global oil and gas sector. Her… A few Nigerian oil and gas companies owe local banks about $7 billion, and the fallout is reaching well beyond those borrowers, according to billionaire Aliko Dangote. Most domestic bank financing for the industry is now on hold, Dangote told the Nigerian Association of Petroleum Explorationists conference in Lagos Wednesday. “A few companies, I believe, owe the banks about $7bn,” he said. “As a result, most funding from our domestic banks is on hold.” Dangote offered no names or breakdown of the debt, nor did he say how much was overdue. Nigeria has some ambitious plans for its oil industry. The government wants crude production at 3 million barrels per day by 2030. The latest numbers, released Wednesday, put October output at 1.51 million bpd, down from 1.53 million in September. Nigeria produced just enough crude in October to meet its 1.5 million-bpd OPEC quota, something it has now managed for six consecutive months. Dangote wants to see considerably more production than that. He called the government’s 3 million-bpd target for 2030 too modest, pointing out that Nigeria once had its sights set on 4.2 million bpd by 2024. The Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission is offering 40 blocks in its 2026 licensing round, saying last month that 22 recent awardees were expected to bring at least 250,000 bpd online within five years. Dangote sees the need for more exploration and local technical expertise and has called for fewer surprises from policymakers. He is also pressing banks to extend more credit to Nigerian-owned operators so they don’t have to chase foreign financing. His 650,000-bpd refinery outside Lagos carried 7.9 trillion naira, about $5.8 billion, in debt at the end of June, after reducing the balance by 798 billion naira in the first half. The refinery’s recent share offering drew 5.85 trillion naira in applications from nearly 3.8 million investors. Dangote did not say whether his refinery’s borrowing was included in the $7 billion industry debt figure. Saudi Arabia reported a 26% increase in October production, while Iraq has also increased output. Those additional barrels have helped pressure oil prices, although shipments remain dependent on alternative routes, ship-to-ship transfers and military protection. Physical crude availability is improving. Normal shipping conditions are not, leaving oil futures unusually sensitive to diplomatic statements and renewed threats against tankers. title: Hudbay cuts cost outlook as Copper Mountain improves
summary: The operating gains come as Hudbay prepares to help finance its Copper World project in Arizona.
body: Hudbay Minerals (TSX, NYSE: HBM) reduced its annual cost forecast again as Copper Mountain generated positive quarterly free cash flow for the first time since the company acquired the British Columbia mine in 2023. Hudbay now expects annual copper cash costs, after credits for other metals, of negative 55¢ to negative 35¢ per lb., down from negative 45¢ to negative 25¢, according to a statement Thursday. The negative figure means by-product revenue more than covers the costs included in that measure. Adjusted third-quarter profit rose 11-fold to 34¢ per share, Hudbay also said, short of the 36¢ average of analyst forecasts. The operating gains come as Hudbay prepares to help finance its Copper World project in Arizona. Gold by-product credits support the lower annual cost forecast, although working capital absorbed cash in the quarter and left free cash flow below BMO Capital Markets’ expectations, analyst Matthew Murphy said. “Despite ongoing inflationary pressures across the mining sector, particularly from fuel and consumable costs, Hudbay stands out as the first company in our coverage to lower its 2026 cost guidance twice,” Jefferies mining analyst Fahad Tariq wrote in a note. “At a time when many producers continue to grapple with cost inflation, the revision highlights Hudbay’s ability to offset industry-wide pressures and further strengthens its position as a low-cost copper producer.” Third-quarter revenue more than doubled to a record $765.9 million, the company said. Copper production rose 25% from a year earlier to 30,152 tonnes and gold output increased 30% to 69,513 ounces. Hudbay also lowered its sustaining cash cost forecast to $1.40–$1.80 per lb. from $1.70–$2.10. Annual production guidance remains 110,000–138,000 tonnes of copper and 217,000–272,000 oz. of gold. Sustaining capital spending is expected to finish $35 million below Hudbay’s $435-million budget. That reflects lower capitalized stripping, capital deferrals and efficiencies. Gold output exceeded BMO’s 59,000-oz. forecast and the 62,000-oz. analyst consensus, helped by higher throughput, grades and recoveries in Manitoba. Copper Mountain’s mill processed 43,500 tonnes a day in September and remains on track for 50,000 tonnes a day by year-end. “Importantly, Copper Mountain generated positive free cash flow for the first time under Hudbay’s ownership,” TD Securities analyst Craig Hutchison wrote Thursday. “We see growing evidence that recent operational investments are beginning to pay off.” Hudbay acquired Copper Mountain in June 2023. The B.C. operation’s turnaround plan included more waste stripping to improve access to ore and work to lift mill performance. However, quarterly copper cash costs of $3.09 per lb. exceeded the company’s $1.50–$2.50 annual guidance range, with full-year costs expected near the upper end. Hudbay reported $201.9 million in quarterly free cash flow, calculated as $313.9 million in operating cash flow before working-capital changes less $112 million in adjusted sustaining capital. The company’s measure excludes growth capital spending. BMO calculated a roughly $2-million deficit, using $215 million in operating cash flow after a $99-million working-capital build and deducting $217 million in capital spending. That fell short of the banks $58-million forecast and the $88-million analyst consensus. The different definitions explain why the company’s positive figure and BMO’s cash-flow miss coexist. Hudbay and Mitsubishi approved construction of Copper World on Oct. 21. The project, about 50 km southeast of Tucson, has initial growth capital of $2.1 billion. Hudbay is targeting first production in the second half of 2029. Hudbay expects its own capital contribution to the project to total about $500 million, starting in 2028. Mitsubishi’s investment, a precious-metals stream and planned project debt would cover much of the remaining requirement, the partners said when approving construction. Hudbay shares dropped 1.3% to C$

title: Tighter regulation not enough to stop importing illicit gold to UAE: report
summary: Even with new regulation implemented in 2023, the UAE has not been able to better trace its gold imports, a new report shows.
body: The United Arab Emirates (UAE) is known to bridge the gap between gold-producing and gold-consuming countries, but a weak regulatory system has led the country to import at least 591 tonnes of illicit gold in 2024, a new SWISSAID report shows. The report used data from 2021 to 2025 and interviewed over 150 stakeholders to get to these findings and recommendations, and better understand the UAE’s role in the global gold market. Despite tighter regulations introduced in 2023 to promote a greater due diligence regarding imports and exports, massive quantities of illicit gold continue to be imported into the country, the report found. Illicit gold includes the metal that was either smuggled to the UAE without traceability or produced in countries with ongoing conflicts, including Russia, Yemen and Sudan. SWISSAID said the findings are important to the Swiss industry, as it is the main importer of gold from the UAE. “The findings of this study are deeply concerning,’ Head of SWISSAID’s raw materials unit, Marc Ummel said. “They show that the United Arab Emirates remains a hub for smuggled and conflict gold.” The 591 tonnes of illicit gold imported by the UAE in 2024 would be worth $74 billion at current prices. It included 453 tonnes coming from African producing countries, and about 137 tonnes coming from countries subject to international sanctions. This represents 42% of total gold imports into the UAE in 2024. The UAE became a top destination for gold production due to its business-friendly regulation and weaker due diligence requirements and penalties for non-compliance, but that also opened up the door to issues regarding illicit producers. Still, the country has made strides to create tighter due diligence requirements for gold sourcing with new regulation being introduced in 2023. The goal was to increase gold traceability and control, but that is still not the reality. Out of the 52 Emirati refineries that were reviewed for their 2023 to 2025 production, only two were fully adopting the new regulations, the report showed. Refineries still have a weak traceability system, receive gold from intermediaries, fail to conduct due diligence and site visits and seem to be regressing on regulation rather than enforcing the new one. The new regulations have increased transparency on how due diligence is performed in Emirati refineries, but it still isn’t enough to improve poor due diligence, especially when it comes to illicit gold, according to the report. In light of the results of their study, SWISSAID is asking the UAE to better apply its regulations so due diligence can actually be performed by refineries and gold traceability can increase for importers. It recommended that the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) put the UAE back on its list of jurisdictions with strategic deficiencies in combating money laundering and the financing of terrorism. It also asked that penalties for non-compliance should be increased or made public, for Emirati companies to share the names of their suppliers of mined gold and for the Emirati customs authorities to increase their controls. While the UAE is the top destination for gold linked to armed conflicts globally, SWISSAID said those conflicted affected areas shouldn’t be completely shut out from imports, as it would hurt the industry and legitimate miners in the region. The non-profit said that with proper due diligence on UAE’s part, those areas can still be a great source and help combat illicit gold. Switzerland is the top importer of gold from the UAE, having imported 420 tonnes of gold in 2024, and has already imported over 400 tonnes of gold from the country in 2026. title: Ivanhoe Atlantic targets Pakistan copper with Mari Energies deal
summary: Robert Friedland outlined plans for equal partnerships and a local office as the Canadian miner enters South Asia and the Middle East.
body: Ivanhoe Atlantic has signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Pakistan’s Mari Energies (PSX: MARI) to pursue mineral exploration opportunities, marking the Canadian development company’s entry into South Asia. Billionaire Robert Friedland announced the agreement Thursday on the sidelines of the Pakistan Minerals Investment Forum . Friedland is the founder and chairman of I-Pulse Inc., a US company that holds a majority stake in Ivanhoe Atlantic. He said Ivanhoe was beginning to establish a local office and expected to sign another agreement Friday. Mari Minerals, the mining subsidiary of Mari Energies, has several copper and gold exploration projects in Pakistan. “We’re forming equal partnerships,” Friedland told reporters when asked about the MoU’s structure and timeline. He said the company is seeking to bring international expertise to Pakistan to accelerate mineral discoveries. While Friedland indicated that Ivanhoe intends to pursue equal partnerships in Pakistan, he did not confirm whether the agreement with Mari Energies would follow a 50-50 ownership structure. The companies have not disclosed financial terms, specific exploration commitments or a timetable for a definitive agreement. The move gives Ivanhoe Atlantic a foothold in a largely underexplored mineral jurisdiction as Pakistan seeks foreign capital and technical expertise to develop its copper and gold resources. Security concerns and infrastructure challenges remain significant obstacles to attracting international investment. Friedland said Ivanhoe intends to draw on its experience in Mongolia, the Democratic Republic of Congo and Saudi Arabia as it establishes a presence in Pakistan. The Canadian mining entrepreneur told MINING.COM that Pakistan’s copper and gold potential is supported by a vast mineralized geological belt extending from Turkey and Iran through Afghanistan and Pakistan into western China and Mongolia. “Pakistan is profoundly unexplored,” Friedland said in an exclusive interview Thursday, pointing to advances in geophysical surveying, remote sensing and artificial intelligence that could help identify deposits more quickly than traditional exploration methods. He said the country sits along a vast mineralized geological belt extending from Turkey and Iran through Afghanistan and Pakistan into western China and Mongolia. The region hosts major copper and gold systems, but much of its exploration potential remains untested. Friedland also stressed that successful mining development depends on local communities sharing directly in the economic benefits, including employment, education and infrastructure improvements. Drawing on Ivanhoe’s experience in Africa, he said community participation is essential to securing long-term support for mining operations and avoiding disputes that can disrupt projects. Pakistan has been courting foreign mining companies to help unlock its mineral wealth, including plans announced last year to offer concessions to US investors as part of broader tariff negotiations with Washington. The country hosts major copper and gold deposits, including Reko Diq in Balochistan, one of the world’s largest undeveloped copper-gold projects. However, the investment push faces significant obstacles. Earlier this year, Barrick Mining (TSX: ABX) (NYSE: B) extended its review of Reko Diq amid escalating security concerns in Pakistan and the Middle East, underscoring the risks facing foreign companies operating in the region. Developing new mines will also require substantial investment in transport infrastructure, energy and skilled labour. Friedland said lessons from Ivanhoe’s Kamoa-Kakula copper complex in the DRC demonstrate the importance of reliable rail and port connections to make large-scale mining competitive. title: Gold Faces Pressure as Real Yields Climb After October CPI Report - FXEmpire
body: Gold kicks off the Thursday session with its eyes on U.S. inflation data, a sharp increase in Treasury real yields, and the market holiday yesterday in the United States affecting the interpretation of price action. The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported on Tuesday that the October CPI rose 0.4% month over month on a seasonally adjusted basis, down from 0.6% in September. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, advanced 0.3%, matching August and September. Energy prices rose 0.7% during October after a 5.2% jump in September, while gasoline increased 1% on a seasonally adjusted basis. In other words, we had seen some easing in the headline monthly inflation numbers, but not a broad retreat in core pricing. For gold, this is not necessarily a bullish sign. Slower headline inflation can reduce inflation-hedge demand and support expectations of a less restrictive Federal Reserve, yet the steady pace of core CPI gaining 0.3% could keep policymakers cautious. The immediate market concern is the change in expected rates and real yields rather than the CPI release itself. Treasuryâs latest daily par real yield curve is for November 10 due to the holiday. The 5-year real yield rose to 2.56%, the 10-year to 2.78%, and the 30-year to 3.17%. These figures were up from 2.35%, 2.63%, and 3.0%, respectively, the previous week. Every new Gold analysis as it publishes, today's technical signal and key levels, live price â on one page. The higher yields, as far as real yields are concerned, increase the opportunity cost of holding a non-yielding asset like gold. The yield curve has also steepened in real terms over the long end, with the 30-year rate above the 5-year. These Treasury figures are derived from TIPS par yields, not tradable security prices, but they can create inverse pressures on gold, with a broad rise in inflation-adjusted yields meaning a significant hurdle for gold. The CPI itself carries a data limitation . The BLS did not collect October 2025 survey data during the lapse in the appropriations bill fight in Congress, so it cannot publish 12-month percentage changes for October 2026 for the series. Goldâs next test will be whether real yields stabilize after the post-CPI increase and whether investors interpret the report as inflation pressure easing or persistent core strength. A sustained decline in real yields, renewed official-sector purchases, or a worsening geopolitical outlook could support the metal. However, higher real rates and stable risk appetite would weigh against it. We are threatening a breakdown below the $3,900 level. Ultimately, this is a market that I continue to fade rallies in, and I would not be surprised at all to see gold drift towards the next significant support level on the longer-term charts, closer to the $3,600 level. I have no interest in buying gold at the moment, but I do believe that, longer term, it will re-enter a bullish trend, offering a buy-and-hold opportunity. title: A shortage of ore is causing a pricing revolution in copper - Mining.com
body: The decades-old system that the copper industry uses to price mined ores is fracturing in the face of an acute shortage. Since at least the 1980s, a once-a-year negotiation between a leading mining company and a large copper smelter has set an annual ‘benchmark’ price that is used across the market to determine how the two giant industries share out the profits of producing copper. But, with annual contractual negotiations coming to a head, the number of deals linked to the benchmark price has already fallen sharply, and is set to drop further next year, according to consultancy CRU Group. The shift is a major upheaval, affecting the pricing of more than $200 billion a year in copper ore, known as concentrates. A similar shift away from benchmark pricing that took place in the iron ore market nearly two decades ago was credited with delivering a profit windfall to miners. Under annual supply deals, miners typically deduct fixed treatment and refining charges from the price of concentrates to cover the cost of smelting them into finished copper. For decades, the first deal reached between a major buyer and seller has served as a benchmark followed by the rest of the industry. Over the past few years, constraints on mine supply — combined with a surge in smelting capacity and fierce bidding by traders — have driven benchmark charges to record lows. But they’ve fallen even further in the spot market, where TC/RCs are now trading at deeply negative levels, in effect meaning that they’re being added to the cost of concentrates rather than deducted from them. As supply negotiations kicked off in London last month, mining executives demanded that any fixed-price deals would need to be set at levels close to the spot market, according to people involved in the talks, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. Meanwhile, smelters warned that they were already facing such deep losses that they’d started cutting output and planned further reductions next year. Miners and smelters are set to meet again for crunch talks during a major industry gathering in Shanghai next week, but the debate over next year’s supply has become so polarized that many in the industry are questioning whether they’ll be able to agree a benchmark deal at all. In a rare move, Wood Mackenzie — which much of the market relies on for supply and pricing forecasts — has decided not offer a prediction for next year’s benchmark. “The challenge this year is that negotiations are taking place against one of the widest divergences between benchmark and spot conditions seen in recent years,” said Anna Xu, a senior analyst at Wood Mackenzie. The upheaval in the copper concentrates market comes after a surge in smelting capacity in China, which now processes more than half the world’s mined copper. For years, being the dominant buyer gave China clout in annual supply negotiations, but scarce supplies of copper ores have placed its smelters in a disadvantaged position. While Chinese smelters are still negotiating over a benchmark deal for next year, much of the industry has already shifted towards deals linked to indexes for spot TC/RCs provided by third-party agencies like Fastmarkets Ltd. and SMM. The trend mimics a shift that transformed the iron ore market in the 2010s, when top miner BHP Group pushed China’s steel mills into deals that gave them a passive exposure to price indexes based on the spot market. The transition, which came as iron ore prices surged on the back of the Chinese infrastructure boom, helped to deliver huge profits to the largest iron ore miners. And as the market has cooled over recent years, China has worked aggressively to rebuild its pricing power. In the copper market, Chinese smelters have been resisting the push to index pricing for several years, fearing a similar margin squeeze and warning that the indexes could be manipulated. Goldman Sachs Makes Stark Fed Rate Call for 2027 - TradingView
body: Goldman Sachs GS is warning that the Federal Reserve could raise interest rates again in March 2027, extending its tightening campaign beyond December as stubborn inflation threatens to keep borrowing costs elevated. The revised forecast presents another challenge for Wall Street, particularly technology stocks, homebuilders and other businesses sensitive to higher interest rates. Goldman now expects a 25-basis-point increase in December, followed by another quarter-point hike in March, potentially bringing the federal funds target range to 4.25%4.50%. However, the bank acknowledges that the second increase could arrive as early as January. The change follows October's hotter-than-expected consumer inflation report, which marked the third consecutive monthly upside surprise. Headline consumer prices increased 0.4% in October, exceeding expectations for 0.3%, while core inflation rose 0.3%, above forecasts of 0.2%. Goldman chief U.S. economist David Mericle believes persistent inflation will encourage policymakers to signal additional tightening at December's meeting. The bank expects inflation to moderate through year-end before renewed price pressures emerge in early 2027. Higher oil prices, tariffs, resilient consumer demand and substantial AI infrastructure investment have contributed to inflationary pressures. Goldman's outlook is less aggressive than Deutsche Bank's, which anticipates three additional quarter-point hikes through March, potentially lifting rates to 4.50%4.75%. Importantly, Goldman has also delayed its expected first rate cut from September to December 2027, with further reductions projected during 2028. The Fed's December 89 meeting represents the next major catalyst, particularly its updated economic projections and interest-rate forecasts. Investors should monitor core inflation, wage growth, Treasury yields and whether policymakers signal additional tightening. Persistent inflation could pressure richly valued technology stocks by keeping discount rates elevated, while higher mortgage rates could weaken housing demand. Bond investors also face risks if Treasury yields rise further. Conversely, softer inflation and moderating energy prices could reduce the need for additional hikes. For now, Goldman's revised forecast suggests investors may need to prepare for restrictive monetary policy lasting considerably longer than previously expected.

title: October CPI signals troubling outlook for consumers - AOL.com
body: U.S. inflation showed fresh signs of persistence in October 2026, raising questions about how long households will have to contend with elevated living costs and putting the Federal Reserve under renewed pressure ahead of its December 2026 meeting. The Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported on Nov. 10, 2026, that the Consumer Price Index (CPI) climbed 0.4% during the month, exceeding economists’ 0.3% forecast. Core inflation, which excludes food and energy, also came in above expectations, marking the third consecutive month that inflation readings have outpaced forecasts. The latest report is particularly significant because it represents the final inflation reading available to the Federal Reserve before its December policy meeting. Although the BLS could not calculate the usual 12-month inflation rate because of missing data from the 2025 government shutdown, core prices increased at a 3.7% annualized pace over the three months through October 2026, the fastest such reading this year. Also read: Hot September CPI numbers, possible Fed rate hikes spark anxiety for midterm voters The food index jumped 0.5% in October 2026 after no change in September 2026, a sharp reversal at the grocery checkout, the BLS reported . Baby food and formula prices surged 5.1%, the largest single-month spike since the agency began tracking that category in the 1990s, CNN reported . Lettuce prices jumped 7.9%, while the fruits and vegetables index and the dairy index each climbed 0.6%, BLS data showed . Beef prices continued rising, with USDA Economic Research Service data showing cattle inventories at multi-decade lows and sustained consumer demand. Ground beef and steak each increased more than 1%, and the meats, poultry, and fish index rose 0.5% overall during the month. Restaurant costs also accelerated, with the food-away-from-home index climbing 0.5%, the BLS confirmed. Thomas Ryan, a Senior North America Economist at Capital Economics, told CNBC that higher diesel fuel costs are now working through supply chains and pushing up grocery prices. Ryan noted that diesel’s effect builds slowly, meaning food costs are likely to stay elevated for months. The shelter index rose 0.3%, accounting for more than 30% of the overall monthly increase in consumer prices, the BLS reported . Owners’ equivalent rent rose 0.3%, while the rent of the primary residence increased 0.2%, keeping housing costs elevated for renters and homeowners . Transportation services rose 0.8% while motor vehicle insurance climbed 0.7%, keeping the cost of getting around persistently elevated. Mortgage rates near 7.18% as of early November 2026 added further pressure for would-be homebuyers already facing higher shelter costs, according to the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey . Medical care costs also rose, with commodities up 0.5% and hospital services up 0.8%, the BLS reported. Core CPI rose 0.3% for the third consecutive month, and EY-Parthenon chief economist Gregory Daco said the breadth of the increase shows price pressures spreading beyond energy, Fox Business reported . The services-sector measure that strips out housing, energy, and food rose 0.4% in October, pushed by transportation, medical care, and insurance costs, Axios reported . Andrew Davis, head of investment strategy at Bryn Mawr Trust, offered a similar assessment in an email shared with CBS News . On November 11, 2026, Stephanie Link of Hightower told CNBC, “Maybe we’re not going to spend $7 trillion on data centers between now and 2030. That was what we were projecting. title: Tech stocks take hit as Huang quits Nvidia - Yahoo Finance Singapore
body: Jensen Huang's resignation as CEO of Nvidia whiplashed markets on Thursday, hitting the AI giant but lifting some of its rivals as investors tried to game out the ripple effects from the shakeup. Jensen, co-founder of the world's leading designer of the chips that power AI models, stepped down in the face of a board revolt following revelations he had two extra-marital affairs, including with a woman accused of spying for China. Chief financial officer Colette Kress will serve as interim CEO while keeping her finance role, and the board will consider internal and external candidates for a permanent replacement. Shares in Nvidia plunged 13 percent at the start of trading in New York before moderating. The stock, a component in both the Dow and Nasdaq indices, finished down 4.3 percent. The tech-focused Nasdaq had a rollercoaster day, pushing into positive territory in the middle of the session before finishing 0.4 percent lower. "Something that's going on here that's kind of helping to mitigate the losses is that investors are recalibrating who benefits if Nvidia suffers," said Briefing.com analyst Patrick O'Hare, who pointed to strength in Broadcom and AMD, both of which gained more than five percent. "That's kind of helped soften the blow of Nvidia's problems," O'Hare said. Other tech companies were mixed. AI infrastructure companies Nebius and CoreWeave slumped 16.8 percent and 6.9 percent respectively while tech giants Amazon, Microsoft and Google parent Alphabet all rose. Some analysts said Huang's departure won't affect short-term AI projects already in the works. But FHN Financial's Chris Low noted that the shakeup at Nvidia comes on the heels of US elections earlier this month that showcased public hostility to data centers. "A slowdown in AI development would be a positive thing from an inflation and interest rate perspective," Low said. "The buildout is a primary driver of demand-side inflation pressures, after all, and the loss of Jensen Huang might not mean the end of AI development, but it could slow its progress." In other markets, oil prices rose after US President Donald Trump signaled less interest in a peace deal with Iran that markets have been seeing as more likely. "We don't need a deal with Iran. Those days have long since passed. We've got their money, Hundreds of Billions of Dollars, and we've got their Strait!" Trump wrote on his Truth Social platform. Frankfurt's blue-chip DAX reached earlier in the session a record high above 27,000 points thanks to healthy corporate earnings and recent optimism about the artificial intelligence boom. South Korea targets 'world's highest performance' sovereign AI model in record new budget
summary: The 2027 budget will rise 12.8% to 820.9 trillion won, and will include a 21.3 trillion won investment into semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers.
body: South Korean President Lee Jae Myung unveiled the country's largest ever budget on Monday, pledging to "boldly invest in AI and future growth engines." Speaking to the National Assembly on Monday, Lee said total spending for 2027 would rise 12.8% to 820.9 trillion won ($610.14 billion), including 21.3 trillion won for semiconductors, physical AI and AI data centers — nearly double the 2026 level. A separate 4.7 trillion won will go toward developing a sovereign AI model with what Lee described as the "world's highest performance." The government also plans to invest heavily into talent, including training 2,000 specialists to "lead semiconductor design and the regional semiconductor industry," while expanding AI education for students, job seekers and existing workers. South Korea has set up university "contract departments," where students can enroll in company-linked degrees that offer pathways to jobs at firms like Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix before graduation. Companies help design courses, provide financial support and recruit qualifying graduates. The record spending plan comes as the International Monetary Fund forecasts South Korea's economy will grow 3.3% in 2026, its fastest pace since the post pandemic rebound in 2021. Lee said the higher spending would result in "virtually no net increase in government debt," with newly issued bonds used to repay existing debt. The budget also increases spending on defense and social security spending for the youth. Defense expenditure is set to rise 8.2% to 73.3 trillion won. "We will rapidly transform into a smart, elite, and powerful military by establishing a hybrid manned and unmanned system based on AI, robots, and drones," Lee said. South Korea's strong economic growth has been driven largely by semiconductor exports as global demand for computing power rises with the AI boom. Exports surged 93.7% from a year earlier to a record $115.3 billion in October, according to data released Sunday by the Korea Customs Service. Shipments totaled $930 billion in the first 10 months of 2026, surpassing the $900 billion mark for the first time. The country posted a $42.5 billion trade surplus in October, with imports rising 36% year on year to $72.8 billion. Lee said South Korea was within reach of $1 trillion in annual exports, citing strong performance in key industries including semiconductors.

title: Fed Overhauls 2027 Meeting Schedule, Cuts Rate Decisions to Seven a Year; October Slated for Strategy Talks - BigGo Finance
body: The US Federal Reserve (FRB) updated and published its 2027 monetary policy meeting schedule on the 12th. Reflecting a measure to reduce the number of times policymakers debate and vote on the Policy Interest Rate from the customary eight per year to seven, the October meeting will be devoted not to rate hike or cut decisions but to discussing broad monetary policy strategy. According to an FRB statement, policymakers will continue to hold Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meetings eight times a year. However, the meeting scheduled for October 26-27, 2027, is positioned as being "devoted to discussing issues surrounding broad monetary policy strategy," and no vote on the Policy Interest Rate will be taken. The year's final meeting has also been changed. The schedule originally set for December 7-8 has been moved forward to November 16-17, where the Policy Interest Rate will be decided. After that, no meeting will be held until January 25-26, 2028, creating an unusual gap. At an October 28 press conference, Chair Kevin Warsh said of the 2028 outlook that "there will be two meetings devoted to strategy discussions and six meetings for policy decisions." At that pace, policymakers would be able to evaluate roughly two months' worth of economic indicators together between meetings. Note: The schedule is considered provisional until formally confirmed at an upcoming meeting. In addition, in the published materials, the asterisks indicating the submission of quarterly economic projections that had been attached to the March, June, and September 2027 meetings have been removed. Since taking office as chair in May, Warsh has not submitted his own projections even once, and the handling of the quarterly projections itself is under review. He has established a working group to review the FRB's information-dissemination practices and strategy, and whether to continue publishing the "dot plot," which shows policymakers' interest rate projections, is among the items under consideration. The status of publications that the market has relied on as clues to the policy path could change. Behind this is a concern that the eight-meetings-a-year system forces reactions to short-term economic indicators. Warsh has explained that while appropriate policy requires rapid, regular, and information-based assessment of short-term trends, it is equally important to secure the time and room for committee members with different backgrounds of thought to strategically discuss major issues from a long-term perspective. Speculation about near-term monetary policy also smolders in the market. According to CME's FedWatch, the market currently sees about an 85% probability of a 25-basis-point (bp) rate hike, with the remainder expecting a 50bp hike. The FOMC held rates steady at its previous meeting, and in September before that it moved to a 0.25% rate hike to curb inflation. Some investors believe the reduction in the number of meetings will create information gaps. With the frequency of policy decisions declining while reviews of quarterly projections and dot plot publication overlap, the opportunities for the market to confirm the direction of policy will be fewer than before. The outcome of the information-dissemination review led by Warsh could influence future moves in interest rate futures markets.
