title: Cisco beats expectations, lifts guidance and forecasts AI infrastructure revenue to double in fiscal 2027 - SiliconANGLE
body: Shares of Cisco Systems Inc. were flat in late trading today after the networking infrastructure giant reported first-quarter earnings and revenue that came in ahead of Wall Street’s expectations. The company also raised its guidance for fiscal 2027, citing strong demand for artificial intelligence network infrastructure. Cisco reported earnings before certain costs such as stock compensation of $1.40 per share, comfortably beating the Street’s target of $1.33 per share. Revenue for the quarter jumped 24% from the same period one year earlier, to $18.5 billion, ahead of the $18.1 billion analyst consensus estimate. All told, Cisco’s net income rose to $4.6 billion, up from just $2.9 billion a year ago. Although the stock was flat in extended trading, it’s still up 32% in the year to date, way ahead of the broader Nasdaq index, which has gained just 9% over the same stretch. Cisco has been pushing to gain a foothold in the AI infrastructure buildout that’s dominating the technology industry these days after failing to capitalize on the generative AI boom in the early days. However, its push has come at a critical juncture, as investors have become increasingly concerned over the prospects of a slowdown in data center building following the Democratic party’s sweeping victory in the U.S. midterm elections. Additionally, there are growing fears about the impact rising borrowing costs will have on debt-fueled data center construction projects. Still, Cisco Chief Executive Chuck Robbins (pictured) expressed confidence in the company’s ability to maintain its momentum. He told analysts on a conference call that we’re still in the “very early stages of a multiyear network supercycle.” He said he’s confident Cisco’s AI networking technology is strong enough to continue to capture a portion of the multibillion-dollar opportunity that presents. “Organizations are turning to Cisco for our trusted, market-defining technology and our expertise to help them scale, secure and optimize their environments for the agentic AI era,” Robbins added. Cisco is also building out its software portfolio with new tools that can help businesses to build armies of autonomous AI agents that can perform work on behalf of humans. It also sells the security software necessary to protect those agents and their underlying infrastructure against cyberattacks. The company said it’s increasing its AI infrastructure revenue forecast for the fiscal year to $9 billion, which would be more than double what it earned in fiscal 2026. According to Chief Financial Officer Mark Patterson, the company is “unlocking significant operating leverage,” and this is what’s enabling it to grow its earnings “much faster” than its revenue. Investors may still be worried about Cisco’s gross margins, though. This has been a concern for many companies, as the global shortage of memory chips has steadily increased the cost of the components that hardware makers need to build their data center infrastructure products. Cisco’s gross margin of 65.6% in the quarter was in-line with the Street’s estimates, but down from 68.1% in the year-ago period. TECHnalysis Research analyst Bob O’Donnell told Reuters that the decline was unlikely to worry too many people, though. “A small dip in gross margin is not a major concern given higher memory and component costs,” he said. He added that the company’s raised forecast and strong earnings and revenue was the main thing the market wanted to see. For the current quarter, Cisco said it’s looking for earnings of between $1.34 and $1.36 per share on sales of $18 billion to $18.2 billion. That’s a strong forecast, with the Street looking for earnings of just $1.23 per share on revenue of $17.88 billion. title: Nvidia scandal draws in Commerce Secretary Lutnick, who reportedly agrees to testify about China chip sales
summary: Commerce Secretary Lutnick will testify before the Senate Banking Committee following revelations about Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.
body: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has agreed to testify before the Senate Banking Committee, as the fallout from ousted Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy intensifies. Lutnick was summoned by Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott amid scrutiny over whether Nvidia could have supplied advanced artificial intelligence chips to Chinese companies and thereby potentially threatened U.S. national security. Huang and Lutnick both received letters on Thursday evening requesting them to testify in separate hearings on Dec. 3 and Dec. 10, respectively. The letter to Lutnick asked the commerce secretary to testify regarding "recent public reports about NVIDIA and the Department of Commerce's role that raises national security concerns." "Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions," Kristen Eichamer, a spokesperson for Lutnick, told NBC News on Thursday. CNBC contacted the Commerce Department for comment. The letter to Huang said that reports about his relationship with the alleged Chinese spy "raise significant national security concerns." Huang has acknowledged an affair with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based company that has bought over $4.8 billion of advanced Nvidia AI chips over the past two years. The scandal, in addition to reports of a separate affair with a senior executive at Nvidia, led to his resignation on Thursday. There is growing bipartisan scrutiny of the Commerce Department Secretary's approach to chip policy and whether his department was doing enough to restrict the supply of AI chips to China. Lawmakers are also questioning whether the department was overseeing Nvidia's exports thoroughly enough Senator Jim Banks has been particularly scathing, saying Lutnick "appears to have used loopholes to allow some of these chip sales to occur," in an appearance on Fox News on Thursday. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass, who will chair the Senate Banking Committee from January, said on Thursday "Secretary Howard Lutnick and Under Secretary Jeffrey Kessler must explain why they have not closed export control loopholes and act today to ensure our advanced technology is not fueling China's military." In a joint letter with incoming Senate Foreign Relations Chair Chris Coons published Wednesday, they said all documents relating to the export of Nvidia chips to China must be preserved. Sen. Ron Wyden, D-Ore. and Rep. Richard E. Neal, D-Mass. told Lutnick they were investigating the approval of sales of Nvidia chips to companies with links to the Chinese government, military and sanctioned entities. Rep. Brian Mast, R-Fla. said on Thursday that Congress needed to investigate the role of the Commerce Department in approving the export to China of AI chips, but added that he had confidence in Lutnick. Criticism is mounting on President Donald Trump 's administration for declining to include over 100 companies highlighted as national security risks on a trade blacklist, including China's AI startup DeepSeek and memory chipmaker CXMT, Reuters reported in June. Lutnick is a long-standing friend of Trump, with their relationship spanning over three decades, and is widely regarded as a close confidant of the President.

title: France October inflation accelerates as energy prices surge, keeping ECB rate hike bets alive
summary: France October final CPI +3.4% vs +3.4% y/y prelim Prior +3.1% France October final HICP +3.7% vs +3.8% y/y prelim Prior +3.4% The final report here confirms a further acceleration in French inflation pressures to start the final quarter of the year. That owes much to another jump in energy prices, which climbed by another 1.9% on the month and are up by 24.1% compared to October last year. The annual estimate is once again after after the estimates for August and September of +16.7% and +21.3% respectively. That being said, core annual inflation also picked up in October in moving to 1.7% - up from 1.5% in September. That comes as services inflation continues to rise further as well, moving up to 2.6% in October - up from 2.4% in September and 1.9% in August. Ouch. With that, it reaffirms that price pressures in Europe's second-largest economy are continuing to intensify and at a rather awkward time. With French growth conditions struggling and fiscal risks mounting, it is making for a rather untimely backdrop for policymakers to be dealing with stronger inflation. As such, that will keep ECB policymakers on their toes in navigating the next steps. For now, the report here will just reinforce expectations of another rate hike in December with markets also pricing in roughly 82% odds of that at the moment. So, there is that to keep in mind as we look towards next year. What does this data measure? Germany's wholesale price index measures changes in prices charged by wholesalers to retailers and other businesses. It offers an early indication of cost pressures in the supply chain, which can eventually feed through to consumer inflation. Why does it matter to markets? Germany is the the euro area's largest economy, making wholesale prices a useful gauge of underlying inflation risks. A sustained increase in wholesale costs could complicate the ECB's efforts to contain inflation, particularly if businesses pass higher costs on to consumers. How does it fit into the current economic landscape? Wholesale inflation has been accelerating, with September's annual increase reaching its strongest pace since early 2023. Higher energy costs and imported goods prices have been adding pressure, making life more expensive for businesses already dealing with uneven demand. Current relevance to markets? Moderate. The key question is whether energy-driven inflation pressures are becoming more persistent, even as oil prices have retreated from earlier highs. Another elevated reading would reinforce worries surrounding inflation and the ECB outlook, although CPI and wage developments remain more decisive indicators for policymakers. summary: Asia’s refiners are back to buying Middle Eastern oil as flows through the Strait of Hormuz rise, freight rates ease from record highs, and Gulf producers are offering their crude at discounts to regional benchmarks. Chinese, Japanese, and Thai oil refiners are increasingly preferring cargoes from the Middle East in recent weeks, even those that need to transit the Strait of Hormuz, traders with knowledge of the matter told Bloomberg on Friday. body: What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… Asia’s refiners are back to buying Middle Eastern oil as flows through the Strait of Hormuz rise, freight rates ease from record highs, and Gulf producers are offering their crude at discounts to regional benchmarks. Chinese, Japanese, and Thai oil refiners are increasingly preferring cargoes from the Middle East in recent weeks, even those that need to transit the Strait of Hormuz, traders with knowledge of the matter told Bloomberg on Friday. Refiners in the world’s top crude oil-importing region are buying greater volumes from Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and Qatar, according to Bloomberg’s anonymous sources. In October, Asia’s imports of crude oil via the Strait of Hormuz jumped to over 7.4 million barrels per day (bpd), up from just 1.6 million bpd in April, tanker-tracking data cited by Reuters showed early this month. This helped boost total Asian crude oil imports to pre-war levels from February. The significant increase in Middle Eastern flows since August has weighed on physical prices of the Gulf region’s crudes, attracting more buyers in Asia despite the high risks. Middle Eastern benchmarks have been weakening for weeks, suggesting an oil glut may be building amid rebounding Persian Gulf exports and global demand destruction amid high prices. Middle Eastern producers are forced to slash their official selling prices to win customers because the surge in Persian Gulf exports is weakening the physical prices of local grades. Moreover, amid high freight costs, the Middle East’s crude oil could only win Asia’s price-sensitive buyers with lower prices. One of the best examples of soaring Middle Eastern flows to Asia is in India, the world’s third-largest crude oil importer. India’s crude imports through the Strait of Hormuz are estimated at 2.1 million barrels per day (bpd) so far in November, exceeding the 1.8 million bpd imported from Russia, according to Kpler data cited by Bloomberg. The Indian government is offering a grant of $546 million (51.4 billion Indian rupees) to support private…
body: What I Cover Tsvetana Paraskova is an energy and commodities journalist who has contributed to Oilprice.com for nearly a decade, covering global energy markets, commodities,… India is looking for private investors to build and operate the nation’s largest strategic petroleum reserve site, which will boost India’s SPR capacity by 80% and cost an estimated $910 million, local media reported on Friday, citing tender documents. The proposed SPR site will be located at Chandikhol in the eastern Indian state of Odisha on the Bay of Bengal, and will be capable of holding up to 4 million tons of crude oil. The Indian government is offering a grant of $546 million (51.4 billion Indian rupees) to support private investment in the facility, The Economic Times reports. Bids must be submitted by February 26, 2027, according to the terms of the tender. Currently, India’s underground Strategic Petroleum Reserve storage has a total capacity of 5.33 million metric tons of crude oil, equal to only 39 million barrels of crude oil, or eight days’ worth of India’s oil consumption. India’s SPR expansion was a strategic priority even before the Strait of Hormuz was closed, but following the supply disruption early this year, the world’s third-largest crude oil importer accelerated plans to build strategic reserve sites. For example, state-owned Oil and Natural Gas Corporation (ONGC), India’s top explorer, will build a new storage site at Mangaluru to hold about 13 million barrels of oil. In the wake of the Iran war and the disrupted crude flows at the Strait of Hormuz, India found itself in search of alternatives to replace the lost Middle Eastern supply. Record crude oil imports from Russia have helped cushion the blow, but India realized it needs additional storage sites to hold commercial and strategic reserves. India is one of the biggest crude oil importers, but also one of the most exposed to supply shocks, as its current maximum reserve capacity can cover only eight days of national oil demand. summary: The most recent inflation reading for October was higher than expected, coming in at 0.4% for the month.
body: At the start of the year, the Federal Reserve was sanguine about the American economy. Inflation seemed to be trending down. The shock from President Donald Trump's tariffs was abating. Economists projected the central bank could lower rates . Instead, the Fed was forced to raise rates in September for the first time since 2023, hiking 25 basis points as inflation, which has run above the Fed's 2% target for more than five years , reemerged as its bugbear. As the Federal Open Market Committee's final meeting looms on Dec. 8, October's consumer price index was higher than expected : 0.4% month-on-month versus the 0.3% predicted in a Dow Jones survey of economists. So-called core CPI increased 0.3% against a 0.2% forecast. Now, traders are certain the Fed will raise rates next month, according to the CME Fedwatch tool . The only question is by how much. Almost 88% of traders expect another 25-basis-point hike. The rest expect a half-point hike. The cost of living has been a top issue on Americans' minds. Vice President JD Vance cited it as a reason the Republican Party lost so much ground in the midterm elections. "We've got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing," Chicago Federal Reserve President Austan Goolsbee said in an interview with "PBS NewsHour " on Tuesday, adding that prices are "on everyone's mind" and calling inflation readings "borderline disturbing." Fed Governor Christopher Waller said Tuesday that a hot inflation report could push him toward advocating for a half-point increase in December, adding this should be on the table if core CPI were "around 0.3%." "The latest CPI print strengthens the near-term case for tightening, even though a 25 basis point hike should be sufficient for December," Chester Liaw, G7 Economist at OCBC Group Research, said on Thursday. Even with a hike, inflationary impulses could remain, Robert Sockin, chief U.S. economist at PGIM, said in a note Thursday. With the Democrats in control of Congress next year, Trump could use executive actions to increase tariffs, Sockin said. Since the labor market remains stable, Sockin said, he doesn't expect rising interest rates this year to derail "significant portions" of the U.S. economy, leaving open the door to future increases. "We continue to expect the Fed to hike rates by 100 bps with the next increase coming in December and quarterly thereafter," Sockin added.

title: Nvidia's Huang Exit Shakes Copper's AI Demand Story as Goldman Trims Price Target - BigGo Finance
body: The resignation of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is rippling well beyond semiconductor trading floors, raising fresh questions about one of the more crowded corners of the AI supply chain: copper. Goldman Sachs has flagged downside risk to its 2027 copper price forecast of $15,400 per metric ton, with the bank now pointing to $14,600 as a potential average, citing AI-related positioning and softer tariff expectations. The shift lands as Nvidia shares extended a slide that has erased the better part of $1 trillion in market value this month, following the board's investigation into Huang's relationships and his departure on Thursday. CFO Colette Kress has taken over as interim chief executive while the chipmaker searches for a permanent successor. Nvidia reports quarterly results next week. Huang's troubles began with disclosures about a relationship with a businesswoman identified as Alice Huang, alleged by U.S. officials to be a Chinese intelligence asset, and deepened after reports of a second extramarital relationship, with a company executive who reported to him. The company has launched an independent investigation into whether foreign intelligence operatives targeted its chief executive. The link between Nvidia and copper runs through the physical build-out of AI data centers. Roughly 65% to 75% of what hyperscalers such as Alphabet Inc. (GOOG) and Microsoft Corporation (MSFT) spend goes toward servers, processors and networking gear rather than buildings. Even so, the longer-term demand case for copper has leaned on the assumption that Nvidia's order book would keep translating into substations, transformers and grid connections. That assumption is now being tested. Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, told Mining.com that a leadership crisis of this kind "would be damaging at any company but is exacerbated by just how strong the key person risk is perceived to be at NVIDIA." The International Energy Agency has warned that "data center investments have grown too large to be funded from company balance sheets alone," a point that cuts both ways for metals demand. When substations, cooling systems or nuclear restarts stall, copper and aluminum purchases tend to shift into later years rather than disappear. Constellation Energy Corporation's (CEG) Crane plant restart, targeted for 2027, is one example of deferred rather than canceled demand. Separately, Huang had already moved to reduce Nvidia's dependence on copper at the rack level. Copper cabling begins to lose signal integrity after roughly 2.5 meters at 200 Gbps, a constraint that has pushed the industry toward optics for longer runs. "You use optics wherever you must, [and] you use copper wherever you can," Huang said earlier this year, even as he described copper as the leading solution for short-reach connections. The company put $500 million into fiber-optic supplier Corning Inc. (GLW), with up to $3.2 billion available through warrants. The funding supports three U.S. plants intended to lift domestic fiber output by more than 50%. That follows roughly $4 billion Nvidia committed to Coherent Corp. (COHR) and Lumentum Holdings Inc. (LITE). Note: Combined Coherent and Lumentum figure reflects total Nvidia investment across the two photonics suppliers. The market reaction has been uneven rather than uniformly negative. Nvidia shares fell 8.2% to a more than 16-month low in early trading on Thursday, putting its market value on course to close below $4 trillion for the first time since July 2025. Short sellers have booked roughly $9.6 billion in paper profits this week, according to data analytics firm ORTEX. Competitors have drawn buyers. Advanced Micro Devices Inc. (AMD) and Broadcom Inc. title: Copper price hits four-month low; focus on demand, AI and US rates - Mining.com
body: Copper prices dropped to four-month lows on Thursday as the market fretted about weak demand, partly due to trouble in the AI industry, and expectations of US interest rate hikes that could mean further gains for the dollar. The selloff accelerated after the New York open on news that Nvidia (Nasdaq: NVDA) CEO Jensen Huang is stepping down, leaving the artificial intelligence industry without its biggest champion. Benchmark copper on the London Metal Exchange was down 1.5% at $13,610 a metric ton at 1705 GMT, but up from an earlier low of $13,515 – the weakest since July 20. A higher US currency makes dollar-priced metals more expensive for holders of other currencies, which could subdue demand. This relationship is used by funds that trade using buy and sell signals from numerical models. US Federal Reserve officials have expressed concern about stubborn inflation and left open the possibility of a 50-basis-point increase at the central bank’s meeting December 8-9. “The inflation print for the US shows that it’s still a problem there, so the metal markets is repositioning around that and it’s dragging down the copper price,” said Panmure Liberum analyst Tom Price. Overall industrial demand for copper was soft and that the drop in share prices of technology stocks was part of the reason, Price added. “Every time AI takes a hit, copper demand and prices come under pressure too.” Elsewhere, the premium, or backwardation, for the cash aluminium contract over the three-month forward climbed to 36-year highs above $175 a ton, partly due to historically low stocks in LME-registered warehouses . It was last around $120 a ton. Aluminium stocks in LME warehouses at 226,350 tons have dropped nearly 56% since January, while in warehouses monitored by the Shanghai Futures Exchange they fell 31% last week to 132,605 tons, their lowest since December. The maturity curve for aluminium prices on ShFE is also backwardated. The November contract SAFX6 was trading at a 355 yuan premium to the December contract SAFZ6. Three-month aluminium retreated 1.5% to $3,022 a ton, zinc fell 1.4% to $3,704, lead slipped 0.2% to $1,879, tin CMSN3 was down 1.2% at $45,985 and nickel gained 0.3% to $16,235. title: World oil market is returning to surplus as Gulf exports recover, IEA says - KELO-AM
body: LONDON, Nov 13 – The world oil market will return to a surplus in the fourth quarter of this year, the International Energy Agency said on Friday, as Middle East exports recover faster than global oil demand despite continued attacks on shipping. The ​agency also gave more details of remaining volumes to come from a record release of ‌oil from its members’ emergency reserves pledged in March, saying 71 million barrels would be made available by the end of February including 15 million barrels of diesel to ease market tightness. Oil supply will average 105 million barrels per day in the fourth quarter, the Paris-based agency, which advises industrialised countries, said in a monthly report, 1.7 million bpd higher ‌than ​forecast demand. The IEA had previously forecast a fourth-quarter supply deficit. “The oil ⁠market is showing tentative signs of ⁠rebalancing, with global oil supplies surpassing demand for the first time since the outbreak of the war in Iran,” the agency said in the report. Oil prices reversed earlier gains after the IEA report was released at 0900 GMT. Brent crude was last down 0.1% at $95.71 a barrel. The report follows ​signs that Gulf oil producers are recovering exports disrupted since the start of the war in late February by using workarounds such as so-called dark crossings through the Strait of Hormuz, where tankers ⁠switch off tracking signals to evade attack. The OPEC+ group, which ⁠includes the Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries and allies such as ​Russia, pumped 41.23 million bpd of crude in October, OPEC said on Wednesday, up about 2.04 million bpd ​from September and 97% of the pre-war February volume. Other ‌analysts have also forecast a return to excess supply, despite the lack of a resolution to the Iran war and continuing tanker attacks in the Gulf. JPMorgan last week forecast a global surplus of 1.4 million bpd in October. High oil prices have also curbed demand this year, helping tip the balance into a ⁠surplus. World oil demand is forecast to fall by 2.7 million bpd in 2026 to 102.3 million bpd before rebounding by 2 million bpd in 2027, the IEA said, little changed from its previous forecasts. As well as rising ⁠output from OPEC+, the IEA flagged supply ‌rising from outside the group. Production from the United States, Canada, Brazil, Argentina and ⁠Guyana will rise by 1.6 million bpd this year, the IEA said. ​In 2027, ‌global supply is projected to rise by 6.6 million bpd to 108.1 ​million bpd, ⁠led by a further recovery in Gulf output. Still, the 2027 supply growth forecast is down 1.1 million bpd from last month’s report, and the lower outlook partly reflects a downward revision from Iran, the IEA said. Iran is subject to a US blockade that has curbed its oil exports. For 2027, the IEA sees the supply surplus at about 3.8 million bpd, slightly down from a 3.94 million bpd surplus last month. (Reporting by Alex Lawler; Editing by Joe ​Bavier, Elaine Hardcastle, Kirsten Donovan)

title: Oil heads for second weekly loss as fears of Middle East escalation ease - سانا
body: Melbourne, Nov. 13 (SANA) Oil prices were heading for a second straight weekly decline on Friday as fears of a wider military escalation in the Middle East eased, despite continued risks to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and an ongoing U.S. blockade of Iran, Reuters reported. Brent crude futures traded at $95.41 a barrel, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate ( WTI ) crude stood at $88.52. The benchmarks were on track for weekly losses of 2.4% and 2.5%, respectively. Concerns over oil supplies persisted following reports of explosions involving tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and claims by the Houthi militia that it had targeted Saudi oil facilities. Prices also faced pressure from an unexpected rise in U.S. crude inventories, which increased by about 4.7 million barrels last week, against analysts’ forecasts for a decline. title: Micron posts record memory profits as AI demand reshapes the chip cycle - Crypto Briefing
body: Revenue jumped 379% in fiscal Q4 2026, yet the stock still trades like investors are bracing for a downturn Micron Technology just put up the kind of quarter that makes spreadsheets look broken. Revenue for fiscal Q4 2026 hit $54.23 billion , a 379% jump from the same period a year earlier. And yet the stock trades at roughly 11 to 14 times trailing earnings. The market is applauding politely while keeping one hand near the exit. The quarter ended around September 3, 2026. It capped a full fiscal year in which Micron brought in $133.19 billion in revenue, up 256% year over year. For the first time, the company’s DRAM revenue crossed the $100 billion mark. DRAM is the short-term working memory that computers and servers lean on to juggle active tasks, and right now AI data centers can’t get enough of it. Profitability kept pace with the top line. Gross margin landed at about 87% in the fourth quarter, and operating margins topped 80%. GAAP net income came in at $37.70 billion for the quarter. Non-GAAP earnings per share reached $33.42. Most of the growth came from Micron’s data center business units, which posted margins between 83% and 90%. The product list driving demand reads like a data center shopping cart: high-bandwidth memory (HBM), DRAM, NAND flash, and data center SSDs. HBM is the standout. Think of it as memory stacked vertically and placed right next to an AI processor so data doesn’t have to travel far, which matters when chips are chewing through massive models. Micron says HBM shipments are expanding across a growing roster of customers. The majority of its calendar 2027 HBM supply has already been contracted, at higher prices than the year before. Daily. Free. Join 34,000+ readers across crypto, finance, and policy. CEO Sanjay Mehrotra pointed to 26 Strategic Customer Agreements, or SCAs, that Micron has signed. These deals give the company visibility into revenue and lock in commitments for a significant share of output through 2027 and beyond. More than 75% of Micron’s fiscal 2027 output is already committed under these agreements. The contracts include price protections and carry substantial remaining performance obligations, meaning customers have signed up to buy a lot of product that hasn’t shipped yet. Supply tightness is expected to persist beyond calendar 2027, which supports the case that buyers are signing long-term deals because they’re worried about getting shut out. Micron isn’t signaling a slowdown in the near term. For the first quarter of fiscal 2027, the company guided revenue to a range of $60 billion to $63 billion. That would top the record quarter it just reported. Management also expects sequential growth to continue throughout fiscal 2027. A trailing multiple of roughly 11 to 14 times earnings is the market’s way of saying it doesn’t fully trust these profits to last. Investors have seen memory upcycles before, and they have also seen what happens when the cycle turns. The worry is familiar. Strong pricing encourages heavy investment, new capacity eventually comes online, and the resulting oversupply can crush prices and margins. The counterargument rests on those SCAs. If more than three-quarters of next year’s output is already spoken for, with price protections attached, a sudden collapse in Micron’s revenue becomes harder to imagine over that window. The key thing to watch is how those Strategic Customer Agreements perform under pressure. Price protections and performance obligations look great on paper during a shortage, but their real test comes if demand cools or competitors add capacity. Micron’s ability to secure the majority of its calendar 2027 HBM supply at higher year-over-year prices gives it a strong position in the fastest-growing part of the market. The risks haven’t vanished. Memory remains a capital-intensive industry exposed to cyclical downturns, and a slowdown in AI infrastructure spending would hit the data center units that now generate the bulk of Micron’s growth.

Microsoft emerged as a new hyperscale customer, joining Cerebras' expanding network of enterprise and cloud partnerships. The agreement creates another potential competitor to Nvidia's GPU-based ecosystem, although Cerebras has not disclosed the Microsoft contract's financial value. The development comes as AMD and Broadcom gain momentum in alternative AI hardware. Cerebras differentiates itself through wafer-scale processors designed for high-speed inference, particularly applications requiring rapid responses from large AI models. Cerebras reported $26.1 billion in remaining performance obligations as of September 30, up from approximately $25.4 billion in the previous quarter. A significant portion relates to its long-term OpenAI computing agreement, which includes committed infrastructure capacity and related services. However, backlog is not cash already received or revenue already recognized. Some obligations also incorporate estimated data-center pass-through costs, making the figure different from future operating profit. The distinction matters because AI infrastructure financing increasingly depends on long-term customer commitments supporting substantial upfront investment. Cerebras has secured 700 megawatts of gross data-center capacity for delivery by the end of 2027, while expanding manufacturing through Flex and Sanmina. Its Oracle partnership will also bring Cerebras-powered inference to Oracle Cloud Infrastructure in 2027, providing another route to enterprise customers. The expansion resembles the aggressive capacity-building strategies pursued by Nebius and CoreWeave , where strong demand must justify substantial infrastructure spending. Cerebras raised its full-year core revenue forecast to $940 million–$960 million from its previous $880 million–$890 million range. For the fourth quarter, management expects core revenue of $310 million–$330 million and a core operating margin between negative 1% and positive 1%. CEO Andrew Feldman also said the company expects revenue to triple in 2027, although execution will depend on computing capacity becoming available. That uncertainty has already affected competitors. Nebius recently cut its outlook after construction delays pushed expected capacity into 2027. Cerebras' growth also arrives as AI stock valuations face increasing scrutiny over profitability and financing costs. title: Nvidia hasn’t selected search firm for permanent Huang replacement, board tells CNBC
summary: Speculation has swirled around who Nvidia's board will select to permanently succeed Huang.
body: Nvidia hasn't yet selected a search firm to work with in identifying a successor for former CEO Jensen Huang , the company's board told CNBC. "We are in the process of selecting a search firm for the Nvidia CEO role," the board said in a Friday statement. "We have not formally engaged any potential candidates." The comments come after speculation has swirled about who might be tapped to replace Huang. Nvidia announced Thursday that Huang would step down as CEO of the chipmaker after multiple reported affairs, including one with a woman purported to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia named CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO and said it will begin a search for a permanent CEO to replace Huang, adding that it will consider both internal and external candidates. The Financial Times reported Friday that Nvidia's board has approached Arm CEO Rene Haas in its search for Huang's successor, citing people familiar with the matter. Nvidia's board said, "Any speculation regarding individual candidates, whether internal or external, is premature." Before joining the SoftBank-backed chip company in 2013, Haas spent seven years at Nvidia, serving in a variety of roles including vice president of its computing products business. Nvidia shares fell more than 2% on Friday, dragging the company's market cap below $4 trillion as investors digested the news of Huang's departure, and the specter of ongoing probes into his conduct. On Tuesday, Nvidia said it had retained Wachtell Lipton to investigate allegations that Huang had been the target of a foreign intelligence effort, following revelations that its then-CEO had an intimate relationship with Alice Huang, who several outlets reported is suspected of working for Chinese intelligence. Three House committees have asked Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on Nov. 18 . The Senate Banking Committee has also requested that Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick testify to discuss "serious concerns about our national security," and how the company's top AI chips have reportedly ended up in China.

summary: The top U.S. commodities regulator in October announced proposed crypto rules to assert its jurisdiction over the asset class.
body: The Commodity Futures Trading Commission is already seeing demand from crypto exchanges planning to opt in to its newly proposed rules governing digital assets, according to Chairman Michael Selig. The commodities regulator in October proposed rules aimed at preventing abuse in crypto markets and codifying crypto transaction rules under a federal rulebook. In the announcement , Selig said the move was a "critical step" in ensuring the United States remains the crypto capital of the world. Speaking this week at Cantor Convergence, an annual FinTech conference held in Miami Beach, Selig told CNBC in an exclusive interview that many of the major crypto exchanges are already registered with the CFTC because they offer financial derivatives, including perpetual futures, on their platforms and would now be able to add spot trading. "We're also getting interest from new entrants who say, 'Look, signing up with 50 different state regimes is tough. We'd rather come to one regulator and get a license at the CFTC' so those new entrants are lining up to come register with us as well," he added. After the Clarity Act, a comprehensive market structure bill that established a regulatory framework for digital assets, stalled in the Senate in September, the CFTC and the SEC moved to establish federal frameworks using their existing statutory authorities. "We need to protect our markets and protect our customers using those markets so we'll continue to do exactly that in the wake of the Clarity Act failing to get the votes it needed to get to the president's desk during the current Congress," Selig said. "Our statute does provide for authority of the agencies to register exchanges that want to offer margined, leveraged, or financed crypto assets or other types of commodity trading so we're utilizing that authority to allow our existing exchanges to begin offering these products under a regulated framework," he said. Selig added that the oversight is opt-in for exchanges that are not currently offering margin leveraged financing, which is not permitted under existing state regimes. But the CFTC's new rules could face new scrutiny and oversight in 2027, with Democrats set to take control of the House and Senate after the midterms. Selig told CNBC he hopes the U.S. won't see a wave of software developers moving offshore, as many crypto businesses threatened to do under the Biden administration. "I really hope that we learned lessons from the last several years in this space," he said. Crypto firms were at odds with Washington during the Biden administration, asking for clear operating rules, while also facing lawsuits brought by the SEC under former chair Gary Gensler's leadership. That shifted after President Donald Trump's 2024 victory. "I do hope that we can work together with both sides of the aisle to protect software developers who want to do the right thing," Selig said, adding that those looking to commit crimes and engage in fraud should be held accountable. When asked whether he's prepared for increased scrutiny from Congress in 2027, Selig said, "Congress will do its job investigating where it needs to investigate." "I'm happy to answer any questions that Congress has for me just as I would answer Congress' questions today as I've done before hearing committees several times already," he said. Selig has also faced heat from Democrats for his handling of prediction markets. In February, 23 Democratic senators sent a letter to Chairman Selig urging him to reverse the agency's greenlighting of prediction markets. The CFTC has sued several states to defend what the agency views as its exclusive jurisdiction to regulate event contracts, which it classifies as swaps. body: The market is increasingly concerned about rising inflation but this is a slight relief, with some bids in bonds afterwards and modest USD selling. We will hear from the Fed's Goolsbee on CNBC momentarily and he recently called inflation "borderline alarming". Ahead of the data, the market was pricing in 28.5 bps of hikes for December, which is a bit over a 10% chance of a 50 bps move, with 86 bps in hikes priced in over the coming year. For background, the Producer Price Index from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics measures the average change in prices that domestic producers receive for their goods, services and construction. It’s released monthly at 8:30 am ET, typically a day or two after CPI, and tracks inflation from the seller’s side rather than the consumer’s. The headline is the final demand index, which covers output sold for personal consumption, business investment, government and export. Services make up about 68% of it, goods about 29% and construction the rest, so it’s far broader than a gauge of factory-gate prices. Markets focus on two core measures: final demand excluding food and energy, and the narrower measure that also excludes trade services. Trade services capture retailer and wholesaler margins, which swing sharply and often run opposite to input costs, as when gas station margins shrink during an oil spike. The PPI is still watched as a pipeline indicator. The intermediate demand indexes for processed goods, unprocessed goods and services show cost pressures building at earlier stages of production before they reach consumers. Its biggest market role today is as an input to core PCE, the Federal Reserve’s preferred inflation gauge. Components such as portfolio management fees, airline passenger services, physician care and hospital services feed directly into PCE, so economists use CPI and PPI together to estimate core PCE weeks before its release. A surprise in those categories can shift Fed pricing even when the PPI headline looks unremarkable. PPI data are revised for four months after initial publication, and the revisions are often large enough to change the trend. Your market education doesn't end here. body: Germany Eyes €4 Billion Buyout of RWE and E.ON’s Urenco Stake Iraq’s crude oil production hit 4.6 million barrels per day (bpd) in October, the highest since 2019, data from the International Energy Agency’s monthly report showed on Friday, as OPEC’s second-largest producer hiked output by 540,000 bpd from September. Kuwait and Saudi Arabia also boosted their October crude oil output compared to September, as rising volumes of oil are leaving the Strait of Hormuz on smaller tankers, which then transfer the crude cargoes onto supertankers in the Gulf of Oman. Iraq’s October crude oil production topped its OPEC+ quota by about 170,000 bpd, showed the data in the IEA’s Oil Market Report for November. Kuwait also boosted its crude oil production last month, from 1.58 million bpd in September to 2.03 million bpd in October, although the Gulf producer was still about 650,000 bpd short of its OPEC+ ceiling. OPEC’s top producer and de facto leader, Saudi Arabia, hiked crude oil production by about 1 million bpd to 9.99 million bpd, up from 8.93 million bpd in September, according to IEA data. Per the agency’s estimates, Saudi Arabia was still producing 480,000 bpd below its OPEC+ quota in October. The Kingdom told OPEC that it pumped 10.563 million bpd in October , back near pre-war levels and slightly above its OPEC+ quota of about 10.5 million bpd. The Saudis, however, noted in OPEC’s monthly report that part of the jump in output went straight into storage, which means Saudi supply to the market for exports didn’t soar as much as production did. Saudi Arabia’s supply to the market (domestic and overseas) was 7.122 million bpd in August, 7.988 million bpd in September, and 9.2 million bpd in October, while production was 6.238 million bpd in August, rising to 8.372 million bpd in September, and to 10.563 million bpd in October. Gulf producers have ramped up crude oil production in recent weeks as crude oil flows through the Strait of Hormuz have significantly increased since August, thanks to shuttle shipments through the chokepoint. body: Germany Eyes €4 Billion Buyout of RWE and E.ON’s Urenco Stake India’s fuel demand for road transportation is nearly a decade away from peaking despite rising sales of electric two- and three-wheelers, as commercial transport and conventional fleets will keep using greater volumes of gasoline and diesel, BloombergNEF has said. India’s fuel demand for road transportation is expected to peak at above 2.5 million barrels per day (bpd) in 2034, research firm BloombergNEF said in its India Electric Vehicle Outlook 2026. India’s rising road fuel demand could sustain global oil demand growth for longer than growth in China, where gasoline and diesel consumption has dropped this year amid demand destruction from higher oil prices and the acceleration of electric vehicle adoption. However, India’s electric vehicle (EV) sales are lagging behind 2030 targets, and the country will need as much as $29 billion of investment in charging infrastructure by 2040 to accelerate the adoption of EVs beyond two- and three-wheelers, according to BloombergNEF. In the India Transition Factbook 2026 published last month, BloombergNEF noted that Indian EV sales are rising but the country is far from reaching most of its 2030 targets. While lower total cost of ownership, greater model availability, and a sustained policy push are helping boost Indian EV sales, only three-wheeler EV sales are likely to hit the government targets. These goals are for EVs to account for 80% of two- and three-wheeler sales by the end of the decade, 70% of commercial vehicles to be EVs, and 30% of passenger vehicles to be electric. “However, BNEF modeling suggests India will fall short of most of these goals, with three-wheelers the exception,” BNEF said in October. “Higher fuel costs stemming from the conflict in the Persian Gulf could improve the economics of EVs, but further measures will be needed if the country is to hit all of its 2030 targets.” Despite being the second-largest car market in the Asia Pacific region, India’s electric car sales have remained modest, with sales starting to pick up only now, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said in its Global EV Outlook 2026. We provide what many… A power plant built at the landfall of the Nord Stream gas pipelines in northeastern Germany was shut down after the pipelines were sabotaged. Now the facility is being dismantled and sent to Ukraine. The Greifswald industrial power plant in Lubmin is majority owned by Germany’s Securing Energy for Europe (SEFE). Adrianne Montgobert, a spokesperson for the state-owned company, confirmed to RFE/RL that dismantling of the plant is currently under way, with its transfer being managed by a team from Naftogaz, Ukraine’s oil and gas giant. The Nord Stream pipelines, which run under the Baltic Sea from Russia to Germany, are no longer operational. The spokesperson said in an e-mail, “all reuse and sale options [for the Lubmin plant] were explored including actual sales negotiations, but no commercially viable solution emerged.” Donating the facility to Ukraine, Montgobert added, was seen as “the best alternative to scrapping it,” after it ceased operation in April 2023. A September 2022 file photo of the Greifswald industrial power plant, beside the German landfall of the Nord Stream gas pipelines from Russia. The facility heated gas arriving through Nord Stream 1 and supplied electricity to Germany’s power grid. Ukraine's energy infrastructure has been repeatedly targeted by Russian strikes in recent weeks in a concerted effort to weaponize the coming months of cold and darkness. The Lubmin facility's transfer is set to be completed within "the first quarter" of 2027, Montgobert said. An unsuccessful motion to halt the plant's transfer to Ukraine was made in May by the main opposition party, Alternative for Germany (AfD), who claimed the plant's removal would "impair future energy policy options." The AfD has supported ending military aid to Ukraine and lifting sanctions on Russia. Gerold Juergens, president of the Western Pomerania Business Association, appeared to reference allegations Ukraine was behind the destruction of the Nord Stream pipelines when he told a German media outlet , "many people's impression is: First they blow up the pipeline and then they take away the power plant. You can't explain that to anyone." The trial of a Ukrainian special forces officer accused of leading a team in sabotaging the Nord Stream pipelines is currently under way in Hamburg. Kyiv has denied involvement in the explosions that ruptured three of the four undersea Nord Stream pipelines in September 2022. Montgobert said the decision to gift the Greifswald facility to Kyiv “has been met with understanding” from the workers who ran the plant. Its dismantling has “proceeded smoothly, with no reported concerns from long-time employees or managers,” Montgobert said. An autotransformer being loaded for shipment from Lithuania to Ukraine in 2023. The transfer of the Lubmin plant is part of a wider EU-led initiative to transfer components of energy facilities, and in some cases entire decommissioned plants, to Ukraine. In September, Lithuania pledged to donate hundreds of tons of hardware from the Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant, which was decommissioned in 2009. In December 2025, the EU completed the dismantling and relocation of a complete gas-fired thermal power plant from Lithuania to Ukraine. The Vilnius Combined Heat and Power Plant was delivered through 149 separate shipments with a total weight of 2,399 tons. It was not reconstituted, but used for parts at Ukrainian energy facilities. title: Copper shortage or surplus? Banks split on 2027 outlook
summary: Deutsche bank warns dwindling supplies could trigger a price squeeze, while Goldman Sachs sees risks from tariffs and investor positioning.
body: Deutsche Bank says copper prices could surge to $10 a pound by mid-2027 as shrinking supplies of readily available metal threaten a liquidity crisis, challenging a more cautious outlook from Goldman Sachs. The bullish forecast comes as Goldman Sachs warns its $15,400-per-tonne copper price projection for 2027 faces downside risks following the US midterm elections. The bank estimates prices could average $14,600 a tonne if investor positioning remains unchanged, or about $14,500 if reduced tariff expectations undermine US stockpiling. “We are probably today in the scarcest copper environment since the 1980s,” Daniel Ghali, Deutsche Bank’s head of metals research, told MINING.COM host Devan Murugan in an interview this week. “The market still is not pricing in the kind of scarcity that we’re seeing.” The competing forecasts expose a growing divide over whether copper’s next major price move will be driven by tightening physical supplies or weakening investor confidence. The outcome could have significant consequences for miners, manufacturers and investors as the market approaches 2027. Ghali said global above-ground copper inventories have probably fallen to their lowest levels since 2006, with much of the remaining metal increasingly inaccessible to buyers outside China and the US. Deutsche Bank estimates that by the end of 2026, only 30% of those inventories will be available for purchase, with the remainder effectively locked within the two countries. Continued stockpiling could push accessible supplies dangerously close to zero, Ghali warned. The shortage is already evident in physical markets, even though benchmark prices have retreated. Copper cathode premiums in Shanghai have reached record levels, while pricing across commodity exchanges points to increasingly tight supplies. Ghali said the disconnect reflects the difference between the amount of copper in existence and the metal actually available for immediate delivery. “It’s not that demand is so strong at the moment,” he said. “We think demand is resilient, but it’s not a demand story per se. It’s actually a liquidity crisis that’s in the making.” The International Copper Study Group (ICSG) offers a contrasting outlook , forecasting that the global refined copper surplus will more than triple by 2027 as smelter production rebounds faster than demand. The projection highlights a distinction between overall supply and the metal available for immediate delivery. While the ICSG anticipates excess refined production, Deutsche Bank argues that inventories concentrated in China and the US could leave buyers elsewhere competing for an increasingly limited pool of accessible copper. The pressure could intensify without any significant acceleration in consumption, Ghali said. He noted that manufacturers are largely buying copper as needed, leaving the market vulnerable if steady purchasing exhausts available inventories. Ghali pointed to the October 2025 silver squeeze as an example of how restricted liquidity can magnify price movements. Once available supplies become sufficiently constrained, even relatively small purchases can produce outsized price increases. Goldman Sachs sees a different set of risks. The bank argues that investor positioning, rather than physical demand, presents the biggest threat to its copper outlook. Concerns that a Democrat-controlled Congress could slow artificial intelligence investment and data-centre construction have made investors more cautious about the sector’s future demand for copper. “The main risk to our forecast stems from positioning rather than physical demand,” Goldman Sachs said in a research note. US trade policy represents another potential catalyst for copper prices, particularly as markets assess the likelihood of tariffs on refined metal. title: Guinea gold mining crackdown leaves 10 dead, sparks exodus
summary: Mass expulsions overwhelm neighbouring countries as Mali warns of a humanitarian crisis and rising regional security threats.
body: Ten people have been killed in clashes between security forces and protesters in Guinea’s northeastern gold-producing region of Siguiri, as a government crackdown on illegal mining triggers mass expulsions and a growing humanitarian crisis in neighbouring countries. The violence erupted Wednesday when defence and security forces attempted to enforce a Nov. 2 ban on unregulated artisanal gold mining , Reuters reported. Protesters erected barricades on public roads before the confrontation escalated into an exchange of gunfire, Guinea’s Ministry of Territorial Administration said in a statement. Five foreign nationals were among those killed, while 13 people were injured, according to provisional government figures. Authorities did not disclose the nationalities of the foreign victims. The unrest highlights the growing economic and humanitarian fallout from Guinea’s efforts to curb illegal gold production in a region where artisanal mining provides livelihoods for thousands of workers and their families. The crackdown has strained relations with neighbouring Mali and Burkina Faso, which are struggling to accommodate large numbers of expelled migrants. Guinea imposed the ban after authorities blamed unregulated mining operations for extensive environmental damage, including the contamination of agricultural land and rivers and the destruction of vegetation. Security forces have arrested more than 1,200 suspected illegal miners in northeastern Guinea, with the first mass trials opening this week in the capital, Conakry. The enforcement campaign has driven tens of thousands of miners and their families across the border into Mali, where authorities have warned of a potential humanitarian catastrophe. About 100,000 displaced people have arrived in Mali’s capital, Bamako, while nearly 60,000 others have gathered in the border town of Kouremale, according to Malian authorities. The Malian government has also recorded 11 deaths linked to the displacement crisis, separate from the fatalities reported in Guinea. Burkina Faso, meanwhile, said Friday it had repatriated 45,406 citizens forced to leave Guinea following the ban. Officials in Ouagadougou have complained that their nationals were subjected to inhumane treatment during the expulsions. The influx of displaced miners has raised concerns that armed extremist groups operating across the Sahel could exploit the growing humanitarian emergency to recruit vulnerable migrants. “These people are vulnerable. We are looking at ways to prevent them from being approached by terrorist networks,” a Malian security ministry official told Agence France-Presse . Guinea, the world’s largest bauxite producer, also holds significant gold reserves exploited by industrial operators including Société Aurifère de Guinée, a subsidiary of AngloGold Ashanti, alongside two semi-industrial companies and hundreds of artisanal miners. Artisanal mining remains a major source of employment across West Africa, where rising metal prices and growing demand for gold have encouraged informal operations, often beyond the reach of government oversight. body: This weekâs gold market has turned on a familiar pressure point. The return available from U.S. bonds rose while bullion offered no yield. The move in rates is measurable, as the Treasuryâs 10-year real par yield rose from 2.63% on November 6 to 2.86% on November 12, a 23-basis-point increase. The 10-year nominal yield also climbed from 4.86% to 5.10%. November 11 was a market holiday, so there was no Treasury observation for that date. Every new Gold analysis as it publishes, today's technical signal and key levels, live price â on one page. Higher real yields lift the opportunity cost of holding gold, and the correction, although not automatic, is one that most traders will be cognizant of. Inflation data offered no clean offset. October CPI rose 0.4% month over month , while core CPI increased 0.3%, matching the prior 2 months. Fridayâs PPI release showed final-demand prices up 0.3% in October after Septemberâs 1.4% increase. Yet the annual PPI increase accelerated to 6.5%, the largest 12-month rise since November 2022. The narrower final-demand measure excluding food, energy, and trade services rose 0.5% for the month and 4.9% from a year earlier. The monthly slowdown is a bit of a relief. The annual and core readings have left the inflation-policy question open, though. Thursdayâs oil rally renewed concern about the Middle East, adding another complication. Gold did not behave as a simple inflation hedge during the sell-off. Higher oil prices have raised concerns that inflation could be a reason for policy to remain restrictive in the United States, while elevated yields and a firmer U.S. dollar weighed upon bullion. The market needs to see real yields turn lower before the safe-haven argument can carry the price by itself. There seems to be support near $3,850, and a hold above there would give bulls at least something to hang their hat on. The rebound has stabilized price after a very fast drop but has not yet reversed the higher-yield backdrop. A sustained move back above $4,000 would improve the short-term picture. Its data could show whether the latest fall produced more long liquidation or new short positions. The Federal Reserve will publish minutes from its October 27 and 28 meeting on Wednesday, November 18 , at 2 p.m. Eastern Standard Time. A more persistent discussion on inflation and further tightening would keep pressure on gold. Evidence that policymakers see recent rate repricing as sufficient could help settle yields to the downside. That being said, the technical analysis for this chart looks rather weak. Breaking below the previously mentioned $3,850 level would be a very negative turn of events, perhaps putting the $3,500 level in focus, as it was a previous resistance level and market memory could focus on that. Total demand is forecast to fall 5% to 1.081 billion ounces, while total supply is expected at 1.045 billion ounces. The cumulative deficit for the last 5 years is estimated at roughly 746 million ounces. These are full-year forecasts, not necessarily audited final totals, but they do describe a market that remains structurally undersupplied without the same degree of near-term tightness as we had seen last year. Metals Focus expects total industrial demand to decline 3% to 640 million ounces. Solar is the weak spot at the moment, as installations have fallen short of expectations, especially in China, and high silver prices have encouraged manufacturers to reduce silver loading or substitute other materials. Outside photovoltaics, however, industrial demand is forecast to rise 4.5% to 492 million ounces, where vehicle electrification, charging infrastructure, and brazing alloys and solders are providing support. This is the better way to look at this rather than calling industrial demand uniformly weak. It just depends on where we are talking. Cumulative deficits are substantial, but the current-year gap is narrowing. Metal released through selling, together with the smaller deficit, has eased physical market tightness. Industrial demand is uneven at the moment. Industrial demand is forecast to rise 4.5% to 492 million ounces, supported by vehicle electrification, charging equipment, brazing alloys, and solders. Jewelry and silverware demand are projected to fall 22% and 17%, respectively, as high prices curb purchases. This split will matter. Silver retains a broad industrial role, but the latest forecast does not supply a simple story of accelerating demand across every potential end market for the metal. title: Gold Makes Worst Losing Run in 4 Decades, Silver Plunge Tests $50 Again - BullionVault
body: The PRICE of GOLD rallied on Friday but failed to reverse this week's $150 plunge, wilting as bond yields jumped on strong US inflation data and extending its worst stretch of losses in almost 4 decades. Down 3.5% from last Friday's finish in London − heart of global bullion trading − the price of gold fixed around $3890 per troy ounce, its lowest week-end benchmark level since the start of October 2025. Priced in US Dollars, that means gold has now matched its 10-in-12-weeks drops of summer 2018, early-autumn 2014, summer 1999 and also twice in 1996, marking the worst such stretch since the 11-in-12 weekly losses recorded in spring 1989. Silver has meantime fallen 9 weeks in the past 12, dipping back below $50 per troy ounce in late-London spot market trade but avoiding a weekly close beneath that level − formerly the industrially-useful precious metal's all-time silver price tops of 1980 and 2011 − at today's 12 noon London benchmarking auction. Down 3.8% from last Friday, that still marked silver's lowest week-end price since the end of November last year, down more than 50% from end-January's all-time Friday high. The London 3pm gold price then set its lowest Friday fix since the start of October 2025. Washington's budget deficit last month blew past analyst forecasts, US government data said Thursday, hitting an October record at more than $400 billion and equivalent to almost 15% of gross domestic product. Inflation in prices for manufacturers and other producers meanwhile held at 5.0% per year excluding volatile fuel and food costs, the fastest pace since New Year 2023 according to Friday's data releases. With headline Producer Price inflation coming in slightly below forecast, betting on Federal Reserve rate hikes into 2027 eased a touch, as did longer-term borrowing costs in the bond market. But conventional 10-year US Treasury yields still traded at 5.13% per annum, higher by 0.27 percentage points than last Friday's finish with the steepest weekly jump since April 2025's 'Liberation Day' chaos . Inflation-protected yields also jumped by around one full Federal Reserve rate-rise, with 10-year TIPS adding 0.24 points for the week to offer new buyers 2.87% per annum over and above the rise in CPI. "There is no silver lining," Reuters quotes one bond-market economist looking at today's PPI data. "Everywhere you look inflation is pushing forward and making the affordability crisis for Americans that much harder." As gold and silver rallied only a little on Friday from this week's strong CPI inflation and Fed 'hawk talk' plunges , US stock markets fell once again, cutting this week's rebound in the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 index to 1.6% as AI chip giant Nvidia plunged another 3.9% amid growing doubts over media claims that sacked CEO Jensen Huang had an affair with a Chinese spy, taking its losses from early October's all-time high to more than 1/3rd. For silver prices, "The bull case increasingly requires investment demand not just to remain strong, but to remain exceptionally strong for years," says bearish analysis from Canadian bank BMO, forecasting that this New Year's record price spike above $120 is driving such aggressive thrifting by solar panel manufacturers that the precious metal's global market balance will flip from a supply deficit to a "record high surplus" by 2030.

Despite the weekly builds, crude was 3.1% below the readings a year earlier, and distillates remain 6.8% lower. The weekly flow picture shows higher activity on both sides of the crude balance. Imports rose 324,000 barrels per day to 6.698 million. Refinery crude inputs increased 322,000 barrels a day to 17.047 million, and exports increased 347 barrels per day to 7.543 million. Domestic production was estimated at 14.013 million barrels per day, up 10,000 barrels per day. The stock build, despite higher refinery runs, reflects the combined movement in imports, exports, and other components. With readings like this, itâs a bit of a reminder that weekly petroleum data can be very volatile. The EIAâs November 10 Short-Term Energy Outlook adds a broader inventory context. It estimates U.S. commercial crude stocks fell to about 410 million barrels at Octoberâs end, the lowest end-October level since 2014. The agency attributes the draw to a wide Brent-WTI spread that encouraged exports and discouraged imports alongside high refinery throughput. It expects inventories to remain below the five-year average through the middle of next year before rebuilding as the spread narrows and domestic production rises. Bitcoin is trading at around $73,470, or roughly €66,250, on Thursday morning, November 12, 2026. What is new today is not a price level but a figure from the network itself: mining difficulty is expected to fall by around 7.5 percent at the next adjustment. That is what the mempool.space calculator shows for block 975,744, which at the current pace will be reached late on Friday evening. It would be the steepest drop since mid-June. What is established: since the start of November fewer machines have been mining bitcoin, revenue per unit of computing power is close to its low for the year, and blocks are arriving more slowly than intended. Our assessment follows further down: the relief for miners takes selling pressure off the market, but it does not replace buyers. Where the price could head over the coming months is covered in our Bitcoin price prediction . Mining difficulty determines how much computational work a miner has to do to find a new block. The protocol adjusts it every 2,016 blocks so that on average one block is produced every ten minutes. When fewer machines are mining, blocks slow down and difficulty falls at the next adjustment. When more machines join, it rises. That is exactly what can be seen right now. On Thursday morning the blockchain stood at block 975,533, with 211 blocks left until the adjustment. Since the last adjustment on October 29, the average time between two blocks has been 10 minutes and 49 seconds instead of 10 minutes. From this delay, mempool.space calculates a decline of 7.52 percent. The figure remains an estimate: on November 9, Hashrate Index was still expecting a drop of 6.5 percent, and the last 211 blocks can still shift the value by a few tenths. The decline follows two sharp increases. On October 16, difficulty rose by 5.92 percent, and on October 29 by a further 5.54 percent to 148.36 trillion. At the start of November, our Bitcoin price prediction on mining difficulty from November 2 was still about growing competition among miners. Two weeks later the picture has flipped: some of the machines that came online in October have been switched off again. The hashrate measures how many computing attempts all miners together perform per second; one exahash is a quintillion attempts. According to the weekly report from Hashrate Index , the seven-day average fell from 1,062 to 979 exahash per second in the week to November 9, a decline of 7.8 percent. The daily figures from mempool.space show the slump even more clearly: on November 9 and 10 they stood at 826 and 825 exahash, and on Wednesday and Thursday back at 984 and 982. That leaves the network well short of its twelve-month high. On November 27, 2025, miners were running at a daily average of 1,245 exahash; today's value is around 21 percent lower. The hashprice is the revenue one petahash of computing power earns in a day, calculated from the block reward and fees. Holding this range could support a recovery and keep the inverse head-and-shoulders pattern intact, which could signal a potential long-term market bottom. However, a break below this zone could weaken the recovery setup. Bitcoin is also testing its 200-week exponential moving average. A weekly close below this indicator could increase selling pressure and push prices lower. Bitcoin could still fall further and form a new low. A break below its previous low would weaken the possibility of a long-term market bottom in 2026. In this scenario, Bitcoin could drop to $50,000 or lower, extending the downturn through the fourth quarter. Another sharp decline could also push Bitcoin into deeply oversold territory, similar to the conditions seen during the 2018 bear market and the March 2020 COVID crash. The current market structure also resembles 2020, when Bitcoin suffered another sharp drop after recovering from a liquidity-driven decline. Ethereum is approaching a key support level near $1,800. Cardano is testing support near $0.17, while Chainlink is trading near levels last seen in August 2020. Solana and other altcoins are also declining as selling pressure spreads across the crypto market. The recent Binance hack and Nvidia’s market weakness have added to uncertainty across financial markets. Speculation on X suggests that Binance futures trading may have pushed prices toward liquidity zones after the hack, while spot buyers absorbed the selling pressure. However, these claims remain unverified. Binance has announced that it resolved the issue. Meanwhile, Nvidia’s recent weakness could reflect changing investor sentiment rather than a shift in its business fundamentals. The company has played a major role in driving market gains over the past two years, making its recent decline another factor weighing on broader market sentiment. Bitcoin’s next move will depend on whether buyers defend the current support zone. The market is showing oversold conditions, similar to previous periods that preceded major price bottoms. However, Bitcoin and Ethereum could still face further declines before any recovery. The $69,000–$64,000 range remains critical for Bitcoin. A recovery above this zone could keep the potential inverse head-and-shoulders pattern intact. body: Benchmark copper futures fell below $13.5K/ton on the London Metal Exchange on Friday, headed for a fifth straight weekly loss—the metal's longest stretch of declines in nearly two years—and on track for the lowest close since mid-July. The copper market is concerned about weak demand, partly due to the turmoil at Nvidia that has cast doubt on the AI buildout, a theme that had attracted investors betting that strong spending on data centers and other infrastructure would boost copper demand. Recent hawkish comments from Federal Reserve officials lifted the dollar, hurting raw materials; on Thursday, Fed Bank of New York President John Williams said U.S. inflation remained "far too high" and policymakers needed to take more action to contain prices. A higher U.S. currency makes dollar-priced metals more expensive for holders of other currencies, which could subdue demand. Copper prices are still up ~8% YTD, helped in part by speculation that the Trump administration may introduce a tariff on imports, although some market watchers have raised doubts on that outlook. Goldman Sachs analysts said they see downside risks to its 2027 copper price forecast of $15.4K/metric ton after the U.S. midterm elections, citing the potential for softer AI-related positioning and reduced expectations for U.S. import tariffs. "We estimate copper would average around $14,500/ton in 2027, with further downside if most of the U.S. inventories built up this year flowed back to the rest of the world," Goldman wrote. Copper futures ( HG1:COM ) recently fell 0.8% to $13,484/ton on the LME, while aluminum, zinc, and nickel also traded lower. Potentially relevant stocks include Freeport-McMoRan FCX , Southern Copper SCCO , Hudbay Minerals HBM , Ero Copper ERO , Teck Resources TECK , BHP BHP , Rio Tinto RIO . title: Capstone cuts copper outlook as restart slips - The Northern Miner
body: Capstone Copper (TSX: CS; ASX: CSC) has lowered the bottom of its annual copper production forecast by 5,000 tonnes after delaying the full restart of its Pinto Valley operation in Arizona until mid-December. The primary crusher needs additional repairs to major mechanical components being manufactured off-site by the original equipment maker, the company said Thursday in an update . Mobile crushers should allow partial processing to resume in mid-November. While the 5,000-tonne impact is “modest,” it “adds to a difficult operational year at Pinto Valley and [the company’s] Mantoverde” operation in Chile, Jefferies mining analyst Tariq Fahad said Thursday in a note. “In our view, the bigger concern is execution, with investors likely looking for improved operating reliability into 2027.” Capstone shares dropped 4.5% to C$10.26 late Friday morning in Toronto, extending Thursday’s 6.5% decline. The company’s market capitalization now stands at about $7.9 billion (US$5.6 billion). The setback puts more pressure on a year-end recovery that Capstone was already counting on. In its Oct. 29 results, the company forecast annual production at the bottom of its 200,000-to-230,000-tonne range, with cash costs at the upper end of guidance. The revised production floor is 195,000 tonnes. Capstone estimated the additional downtime would reduce this year’s copper output by about 5,000 tonnes, depending on restart timing. Temporary mobile crushers could support throughput of up to 40,000 tonnes daily during the interim restart. That would be about two-thirds of Pinto Valley’s nominal milling capacity. The open-pit operation, about 130 km east of Phoenix, has a 60,000-tonne-per-day concentrator and produces copper and molybdenum concentrates as well as copper cathode. Capstone is also grappling with the effects of a national strike in Chile. Called by Chilean trucking groups and a civic movement to protest high fuel prices, the stoppage threatens concentrate and cathode shipments and deliveries of fuel and sulphuric acid, Capstone said Thursday. Preventive measures and on-site storage have so far protected output at Capstone’s two Chilean operations, the company added. Sulphuric acid is used to leach copper from ore, while fuel powers mining equipment. Together with the delays at Pinto Valley, the Chilean truckers’ strike introduces “incremental downside risk to year-end production,” TD Securities mining analyst Craig Hutchison said in a note. At National Bank Financial, mining analyst Shane Nagle cut his rating on Capstone to sector perform from outperform, citing the “near-term operational uncertainty.” Consistent operational performance at Mantoverde and Pinto Valley “will be important to supporting a re-rating which has been materially impacted by [Thursday’s] release,” he said. Pinto Valley produced 6,358 tonnes of copper in the third quarter, compared with 9,949 tonnes a year earlier. Its nine-month output was 27,115 tonnes, down from 30,960 tonnes, Capstone reported in October. The plant had restarted with mobile crushers on Oct. 1 before primary crusher commissioning began Oct. 21. Additional repairs were then identified. Capstone was looking to higher grades at Mantoverde and Mantos Blancos, alongside completion of the Mantoverde concentrator expansion tie-in, to lift fourth-quarter production. Group output totalled 45,218 tonnes in the third quarter, down 18% from a year earlier. The company agreed in September to sell its Cozamin mine in Mexico to Luca Mining (TSXV: LUCA) for up to $385 million (C$549 million). Closing was expected in the fourth quarter, subject to conditions and approvals, Capstone said in October. The sale would add financial flexibility for the company’s growth projects. Capstone’s annual production target includes a full year of Cozamin output.
