title: Dow rises as US stocks gain despite Nvidia losses and Bitcoin slump - TradingView
body: US stocks opened higher on Friday as investors assessed softer-than-expected producer inflation data and a partial recovery in Nvidia shares following a turbulent week for the artificial intelligence sector. The October Producer Price Index (PPI) rose 0.3% month over month, below economists' expectations of a 0.4% increase. The reading offered some relief to investors concerned about persistent inflation and the Federal Reserve's interest rate outlook. The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 143 points. The S&P 500 gained 0.13% while the Nasdaq Composite fell 0.13%. The gains followed a volatile session on Thursday, when the major indexes retreated amid concerns surrounding Nvidia's leadership change and the broader AI trade. The latest inflation data helped lift sentiment ahead of the market open, although the annual increase in producer prices remained elevated. The PPI rose 6.5% from a year earlier, marking its largest annual increase since November 2022. The monthly reading was nevertheless below the 0.4% increase forecast by economists. The data comes as traders anticipate another interest rate increase from the Federal Reserve in December. Markets are fully pricing in a rate hike next month, with expectations centred on a 25-basis-point increase. However, the possibility of a larger 50-basis-point move remains in focus. According to CME's FedWatch tool, the probability of such an increase stood at 10.7%. The latest producer inflation figures may ease some concerns about the pace of monetary tightening, but the annual price increase suggests inflationary pressures remain significant. Nvidia shares fell 0.88% on Friday after losing approximately 11% over the week through Thursday. The chipmaker has faced considerable pressure following the resignation of founder and chief executive Jensen Huang. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was named interim CEO as the board began searching for a permanent replacement. The leadership change has raised questions about the company's future direction and the potential implications for the broader AI industry. Nvidia plays a central role in the sector, while its financing arrangements with other AI companies could also attract greater scrutiny. Despite the concerns, the recovery in Nvidia shares helped support sentiment towards technology stocks. Cerebras also gained more than 16% after raising its 2026 revenue forecast and announcing Microsoft as a customer. Microsoft shares, meanwhile, dipped 1.32% following an outage affecting Outlook and Teams that lasted more than 12 hours. Corporate earnings have provided some support to equities despite the recent volatility. Of the 450 S&P 500 companies that had reported results by Thursday, 83.6% had exceeded analyst expectations, according to LSEG Data and Analytics. However, investors continue to monitor geopolitical developments and their potential impact on financial markets. Oil prices remained higher for a third consecutive session after US President Donald Trump said Washington did not need an agreement with Iran. The comments have raised concerns about the possibility of prolonged conflict and further disruption to energy supplies. Coinbase and Strategy declined between 1% and 3%. Bitcoin fell below $70,000 for the first time since August. Despite the week's turbulence, the major US indexes remained on course for weekly gains. The Nasdaq was set for a 3.2% advance, while the S&P 500 was poised to gain 2.9%. All three indexes were heading towards their strongest weekly performances since early August. title: The Global Economy Is Forecast to Grow 2.8% in 2027 as Oil Prices Decline - Goldman Sachs
body: We harness every resource, insight, relationship, and competitive advantage to drive superior results for our clients. We invest the power of Goldman Sachs' financial and intellectual capital to advance enduring economic growth and opportunity. Goldman Sachs Research expects steady global economic growth in 2027, as lower energy prices and still-strong capital expenditures in artificial intelligence (AI) outweigh tighter financial conditions and more neutral fiscal policy. Global GDP is predicted to increase 2.8% in 2027, up from 2.7% this year, Jan Hatzius, chief economist and head of Goldman Sachs Research, writes in a report. The economies of the US, Japan, and the UK are among those projected to grow faster than the consensus of economist estimates. As has been the case for the last several years, our economists are more optimistic than consensus on US economic expansion owing to resilient investment. They are more downbeat on the European growth outlook amid tighter financial conditions and their expectation that higher energy prices will start to bite this winter. Goldman Sachs Research also forecasts continued robust economic expansion in South Korea and Taiwan, reflecting another year of strong AI exports. While growth is expected to be solid, the risks to Goldman Sachs Research’s forecast for global GDP growth “are tilted to the downside,” Hatzius writes. Renewed escalation in the Iran war could result in another energy price surge. Large fiscal deficits could push up long-term yields more sharply, especially in France. AI capex could be lower than expected because of capacity constraints, regulation, credit market stress, or weaker demand, and Hatzius also sees early signs that AI adoption is weighing on the job market. “We expect another year of solid but unremarkable GDP growth in 2027, but several of the impulses that shaped global growth in 2026 will look different,” Hatzius writes. The headwind from the energy supply shock will likely flip next year as energy prices normalize. The baseline forecast from Goldman Sachs Research’s commodity strategists is that continued Middle East supply adaptation will lower Brent prices to $78 per barrel by the end of 2027, with a similar normalization in global prices for liquefied natural gas. At the same time, Goldman Sachs Research sees an ongoing drag from energy prices in Europe from delayed energy cost pass-through to consumers. How financial conditions and the fiscal outlook will affect GDP growth Lower energy prices should outweigh the effect of tighter financial conditions and a smaller fiscal impulse to GDP expansion in 2027, Hatzius writes. Goldman Sachs Research’s Financial Conditions Index implies a moderate drag on growth over the next few quarters. While our economists do not “expect meaningful fiscal consolidation” in 2027, the large fiscal expansions of the last few years are fading. The main exception is in Japan, where consumption tax cuts, increased defense spending, and the government’s investment plans are forecast to boost GDP growth by 0.7 percentage point. “We also expect modestly positive impulses in Germany and the US—where the Democratic victory in November’s US election suggests some of the spending cuts from the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act will be reversed,” Hatzius writes. title: Posthaste: Mark Carney’s budget spending could lead to higher interest rates, economists say - Yahoo! Finance Canada
body: Mark Carney's second budget could wind up boosting demand and inflation since it includes $152 billion in new spending, leading the Bank of Canada to hike interest rates, says a report by Oxford Economics Ltd. "Overall, new measures in the 2026 federal budget add to what was already shaping up to be a significant dose of fiscal stimulus from last year's federal and provincial budgets and this year's federal spring economic statement," Tony Stillo, director of Canada Economics, and Michael Davenport, a senior economist, at Oxford, said in the report. They said more government spending coupled with rising public and private investment in infrastructure and defence will suction up economic slack faster than previously thought and could result in output undershooting demand. That could lead to hotter inflation, which could push the Bank of Canada to increase rates in 2027 and 2028, they said. "Our modelling doesn't show much of a near-term inflationary impact from the fiscal plan, but it suggests the federal budget tilts the balance of risks towards more rate hikes by the Bank of Canada," they said. Stillo and Davenport are calling for the central bank to hike rates by 25 basis points to 2.75 per cent at its December meeting, following a similar hike to 2.5 per cent in October. They then expect policymakers to step to the sidelines for the first half of next year as inflation slows on cooling oil prices, but resume hiking in the second half of 2027 and into 2028, "particularly if government measures to stimulate investment lead to an even larger upcycle in capital spending or tighter labour market than we anticipate." They are calling for the unemployment rate to fall to six per cent by early 2028. They also increased their forecasts for gross domestic product by 0.4 percentage points to 1.7 per cent in 2027 and by 0.2 percentage points to 2.3 per cent in 2028. One major criticism Stillo and Davenport have about the budget is that it contains little "wiggle room" for lower-than-expected oil prices "The federal budget missed an opportunity to use the revenue windfall to improve the government's fiscal position and leave 'dry powder' as a contingency for unforeseen events down the road," they said. "Instead, the federal government opted to roll the anticipated revenue improvement into new measures and leave less flexibility to achieve its fiscal anchors should its revenue projections undershoot in the future — an outcome we think is likely." Instead of using the increased money from elevated oil prices due to the United States' war on Iran to reduce debt, the government decided to spend most of it on a five-year plan to fund tax incentives, top up grocery benefits for consumers and spend more on defence, social housing and infrastructure. The government said their targets for the debt and the deficit will largely remain on track, but Stillo and Davenport doubt those estimates since they believe Ottawa overestimated the future price of oil in the budget. Canadians returned from 1.9 million trips to the U.S. in October, a three per cent increase from the same month in 2025, according to Statistics Canada's monthly travel data. title: Fed's Logan (2026 voter) does not comment on monetary policy or economic outlook - Newsquawk
body: Fed's Logan (2026 voter) does not comment on monetary policy or economic outlook. A Fed official speaking without touching policy or the outlook is a non-event by design, and wires flagging the absence of comment are standard practice when a scheduled appearance carried some risk of remarks on the economy. The practical read is that the speaker list and topic gave markets no new information, so any positioning built around the appearance unwinds to the pre-speech baseline rather than repricing. Logan has historically sat toward the more hawkish end of the committee, which is why her appearances draw attention in the first place; silence removes that tail risk rather than adding signal. Episodes of this kind tend to matter only insofar as they shift focus to the next scheduled Fed speakers and the blackout calendar around upcoming meetings. The tell going forward is whether other officials fill the gap with substantive comment or whether the committee is collectively quiet ahead of a decision, the latter pattern being the more informative one for the front end.

title: Mass smuggling of up to 1.5 million Nvidia AI GPUs could be the underlying cause of Jensen Huang's departure, leading analysts claim — more than 1.5 gigawatts of banned chips tracked to China despite export controls - Tom's Hardware
body: Over 1.5 GW of Nvidia hardware subject to U.S. export restrictions ultimately ended up in China in recent years, according to SemiAnalysis' Accelerator Model, which tracks AI accelerator production and destinations. The estimate excludes processors that Nvidia specifically developed to comply with U.S. export rules, such as the H20 or H800. The firm also claims that the U.S. Department of Commerce has reached a similar conclusion about the scale of unauthorized shipments. Yet, SemiAnalysis does not disclose the exact number of accelerators shipped to China illegally, or their split between Nvidia's product generations. The scale of the alleged diversions is particularly notable because modern AI accelerators require substantial power and infrastructure. While the report does not explain how it converts accelerator quantities into power figures, it is likely that the company uses package-level nameplate/rated power multiplied by the number of GPUs. Assuming that all of these AI GPUs were Nvidia H200 SXM rated for up to 700W, then China got around 2.142 million of such accelerators, while if all of these processors were B200 SXM rated for up to 1,000W, then we are talking about 1.5 million units. For a mixed deployment, the total would fall between these figures, depending on the proportion of H200 and B200 accelerators. To put these numbers into context, xAI's Colossus One had 220-230,000 Hopper H100 and H200 GPUs, whereas the Colossus 2 has a target of 1.2 million Blackwell B200 and B300 GPUs. That said, 1.5 GW of restricted Nvidia hardware in China represents an enormous amount of computing infrastructure, which is comparable, or even exceeds, the scale of xAI's entire existing Colossus operation. While SemiAnalysis did not reveal all the cases in which restricted AI accelerators reached the People's Republic of China, it supports its assessment with two well-known cases of alleged GPU smuggling. The first involves Supermicro co-founder Wally Liaw, Taiwan sales executive Steven Chang, and contractor Willy Sun, who were charged in March 2026. According to the indictment, approximately $2.5 billion worth of servers were sold to a company in Southeast Asia, with $510 million worth of equipment subsequently diverted to China and obtained by Alibaba . Prosecutors allege that the defendants used substitute servers and transferred identification labels to conceal the actual destinations of the hardware during audits. The second case involves nine individuals associated with Nvidia, Albatron, Chief Telecom, Flying Tiger, and Supermicro in Taiwan. The authorities accuse the group of arranging unauthorized exports of 130 Nvidia B300-based servers, 74 of which eventually reached China. The suspects used shell companies, forged documents, and declared Japan as the destination for servers that were actually bound for China, according to prosecutors. Taiwanese authorities discovered the operation during a drug smuggling investigation. Both cases are still before the courts. Amidst the ongoing fallout and reports into Jensen's Huang's extramarital affair with Alice Huang, an alleged Chinese intelligence asset who was an executive at Megaspeed, one report claims that Ms. Huang was personally responsible for facilitating the smuggling of $7.5 billion of Nvidia AI hardware into China , around 240,000 GPUs, mostly H100 and H200 models. SemiAnalysis suggests that the scale of these violations may explain why Huang's personal conduct became a major issue at this very point in time. The company's analysts speculate that some members of the U.S. intelligence community sought to remove Jensen Huang because he opposed more aggressive restrictions on China's access to American AI hardware. However, the report provides no direct evidence that intelligence agencies influenced Nvidia's board or that Huang participated in unauthorized exports. title: Here are 5 new share price forecasts for Nvidia after the Huang scandal - Yahoo Finance UK
body: Retail investors have been piling into Nvidia ( NASDAQ: NVDA ) shares this week. It's easy to see why – Nvidia's share price is down heavily after Jensen Huang's exit and the stock looks cheap. However, before you follow the crowd and rush to buy, be aware that Wall Street analysts are adjusting their price targets for the stock. All of a sudden, sell-side sentiment towards the AI powerhouse is far less bullish. One of the biggest price target adjustments in recent days has come from investment banking and capital markets specialist Baird. It has slashed its target from $500 to $200. This move came on 11 November, the day before Huang's resignation. Baird's analysts cited a cloud of policy and leadership uncertainty around the company as a key driver of the price target reduction. Another massive downgrade has come from Bernstein SocGen. Its analyst Stacy Rasgon – who is regarded as a leading chip expert on Wall Street – has just taken his Nvidia target down to $200 from $400. Rasgon reckons the company shouldn't have major issues operating during a search for new leadership. However, he says there's uncertainty around who will take over… and what else may be uncovered. At RBC Capital, analysts have taken their Nvidia price target down to $230 from $330. They see limited impact to near-term business fundamentals, noting demand's currently outpacing supply by around 50%. However, they've said that the longer-term impact from Huang's exit shouldn't be underestated given his singular vision, execution track record, and technology acumen. These factors were central to Nvidia's dominance. At Stifel , analysts have lowered their price target to $205 from $315. That's around 13 times fiscal 2028 estimated earnings per share of $15.65. Previously, the analysts had the stock at 20 times 2028 earnings. However, due to uncertainty over who will lead the company, the timeline, retention of senior leadership, and channel and export-compliance posture, they see the lower earnings multiple as more appropriate. Finally, Melius has cut Nvidia from $315 to $185. Its analyst Ben Reitzes has also downgraded the stock from Buy to Hold. Before the recent mess, Reitzes was very bullish on the name. However, the leader's exit has changed things and Reitzes believes potential actions, such as pre-announcing a strong quarter, reiterating fiscal 2028 guidance for 70% growth, increasing the buyback, or announcing a management continuity plan involving the CFO, won't address long-term issues. From these new price targets, we can see that Wall Street analysts are now far less bullish on Nvidia shares than were a few weeks ago. Clearly, the uncertainty around leadership has knocked sentiment. That said, all of the price targets above are higher than the current share price. So analysts don't see the stock falling further given its low valuation today. To my mind, the main takeaway is that investors should temper their expectations. Ultimately, the outlook for Nvidia's changed. The growth stock could still be worth considering. However, don't expect it to fly to $300 in the next 12 months.
